Modules 1 & 3 — Complete Unit Compendium

Product development and special-purpose architectures, broken into 15 units, with every architecture diagram lifted from the decks, all three CAT-1 questions answered in the official key format, and 80+ theory and situation-based questions with full model answers.

Sources ESD Module 1 (125 slides) · BCSE305L Module 3 (49 slides) PYQ CAT-1 Aug 2026, D1+TD1 — Q1, Q2, Q5 Companion Module 2 compendium

How to use this

Modules 1 and 3 are examined completely differently from Module 2. There is no Arduino code here. Every mark comes from a diagram, a table, or a justified choice. This compendium is built around that.

PartWhat it gives you
DiagramsThe deck's own architecture figures, extracted at full resolution — draw from these
ConceptWhat the slides say, in the order an answer needs it
Key pointsYellow boxes — the facts and phrases that earn marks
Theory questions"Explain X with a neat diagram" — the K1 and K2 recall pattern
Situation questions"You are designing X. Choose and justify…" — the pattern that actually appears on your paper
The single most valuable habit for these two modules

Draw the diagram first, then write around it. In a K1 question the block diagram is typically 3–4 of the 10 marks and takes two minutes. Students who write prose first often run out of time and lose the easiest marks on the paper.

What the CAT actually asked

Your CAT-1 drew three of its five questions from these two modules — 30 of the 50 marks.

QTaskModuleUnitCOBT
1Describe the ARM architecture with a neat block diagram and explain its key features1U91K1
2Use the top-down embedded design approach to design an electronic weighing machine; choose microcontroller, memory and components and justify1U31K2
5Choose the appropriate microcontroller and memory for an agricultural drone; block diagram, working, justification3U112K2
The pattern to internalise

One K1 recall question (reproduce an architecture) and two K2 application questions (apply a framework to a new product). Neither K2 question requires you to invent anything — you walk a known procedure over an unfamiliar product. That means both are fully preparable in advance.

The K1 question rotates between ARM7, 8051 and PIC. Prepare all three block diagrams; they are the cheapest marks available.

The four question types these modules generate

TypeLooks likeMarks style
T — Theory"Explain / describe X with a neat block diagram"10
S — Situation"You are designing X. Which processor and memory would you choose? Justify."10
C — Comparison"Differentiate A and B" / "Compare GPP, ASIP and ASIC"5–10
D — Design"Use the top-down approach to design X, with block diagram and justification"10

The three answer templates

Reverse-engineered from your official answer key. Reproducing the structure earns marks independently of content, because the examiner scans for headed sections.

Template A — Describe an architecture (Type T, used by Q1)

IntroductionTwo or three lines: what it is, who made it, what class of device.

Block diagramNeat, labelled, captioned Figure N. Draw with a ruler. Typically 3–4 of the 10 marks.

Explanation of blocksOne bullet per block. Every box you drew must be named; nothing you did not draw.

Key featuresA bulleted list under its own heading — the question asks for them explicitly.

ApplicationsOne or two lines. Cheap marks, always include.

Template B — Top-down design of a product (Type D, used by Q2)

IntroductionWhat the product does and why it is an embedded system.

Top-down design flow diagramThe six-box chain. Identical for every product — memorise once, reuse forever.

System requirementsSplit explicitly into functional and non-functional.

Functional specificationTurn each requirement into a measurable number.

Hardware / software architectureThe system block diagram, captioned.

Component selection tableThree columns — Component | Choice | Justification. The heart of the answer.

Implementation, integration and testing, validationTwo or three lines each.

JustificationA closing paragraph under its own bold heading.

Template C — Choose processor and memory (Type S, used by Q5)

IntroductionWhat the system is and what makes it demanding — real-time, safety-critical, battery-powered.

Block diagramSensors left, processor centre, actuators and comms right, power and memory below.

WorkingHow data flows through that diagram, in four to six numbered steps.

Processor selectionName a real part, then a spec table: core, clock, FPU, timers/PWM, interfaces, power.

Memory selectionFlash for firmware, SRAM for run-time data, EEPROM for calibration, external for logging.

Selection criteria tableTwo columns — Criterion | Justification. The key uses ten rows. Match that density.

ConclusionTie the choice back to the application's hardest constraint.

The closing move that the official key makes every time

The key ends Q2 with a heading literally called Justification, and the paragraph makes two moves: the ATmega328P is sufficient because the task needs only moderate computation, low power and few peripherals; and the HX711 was necessary because it beats the internal ADC. Copy that two-move structure — defend the cheap choice, then defend the expensive one.

UNIT 01

What Is an Embedded System

Module 1 · slides 3–17  ·  Types: T, C, S  ·  Weight: medium  ·  Supplies the vocabulary every later answer reuses

The definition — learn it word for word

Slide 4, quotable

"An embedded system is a combination of computer hardware and software, designed for a specific function or functions within a larger system."

Embedded system = Hardware + Software, designed for a specific purpose.

Two phrases in that sentence do all the work. "Specific function" distinguishes it from a PC, which runs anything. "Within a larger system" is why it is called embedded — the computer is a component of a washing machine or a car, not a product in itself.

The general block diagram (slide 10)

Four blocks around one control unit. Every design question in either module is this diagram with specific parts substituted, so draw it once and reuse the shape.

Purpose of an embedded system (slide 11)

Each embedded system serves one or a combination of these tasks:

PurposeExample
Data collection / storage / representationData logger, digital camera
Data communicationRouter, Bluetooth module
Data (signal) processingDSP in a camera, audio codec
MonitoringPatient monitor, boiler temperature monitor
ControllingWashing machine, air conditioner
Application specific user interfaceATM keypad and display, mobile handset

Application domains (slide 12)

Home appliances · consumer electronics · home automation and security · computer components · automotive · health care · military · industrial · business · retail · communications · avionics · banking.

General purpose computing system vs embedded system (slide 13)

#General purpose computing systemEmbedded system
1Combination of generic hardware and a general purpose OS for executing a variety of applicationsCombination of special purpose hardware and an embedded OS for a specific set of applications
2Contains a General Purpose Operating System (GPOS)May or may not contain an operating system
3Applications can be modified by the userFirmware is pre-programmed and non-modifiable by the end user
4Performance is the key deciding factor — "faster is better"Application-specific requirements — performance, power, memory, cost — are the deciding factors
5Need not be deterministic in execution behaviourExecution behaviour is deterministic for hard real-time systems (missile guidance, airbag)
6Personal computer, laptopDVD player, digital camera
This table is a complete 10-mark answer on its own

"Differentiate general purpose computing systems and embedded systems" is one of the most commonly set questions in this module. Six rows, learn them in order. Row 4 and row 5 are the two that most students omit and are worth the most.

Characteristics of embedded systems (slides 15–17)

CharacteristicWhat it means in practice
Sophisticated functionalityComplex behaviour from a small, dedicated design
Real-time operationsCorrectness depends on when the answer arrives, not just what it is
Low manufacturing costUsually cost-sensitive, produced in volume
Low power consumptionBattery life or thermal limits dominate
Application dependent processorNot the general purpose processor found in a computer
Restricted memoryKilobytes, not gigabytes
Dedicated to specific tasksThe firmware does one job
Wide array of processorsSupported by many processor architectures
Specialised tools and methodsCross-compilers, in-circuit debuggers
Software failure is more severeNo user to restart it; failure may be physical
Extreme environmentsTemperature, vibration, dust
Fewer system resourcesLimited RAM, no disk, no MMU on small parts
Real Time Operating SystemWhere scheduling guarantees are required

Theory and situation questions

Q1.1   Type T  ·  10 marks

Define an embedded system and explain its general block diagram, purposes and characteristics

Model answer

Definition

An embedded system is a combination of computer hardware and software designed for a specific function or functions within a larger system. Unlike a general purpose computer it is dedicated to a single application, and its firmware is fixed at manufacture.

Block diagram

(Draw the slide-10 diagram: a central control unit — microprocessor or microcontroller — surrounded by input devices, output devices, communication devices and a user interface.)

Explanation of blocks

  • Control unit (µP / µC) — executes the firmware and coordinates all other blocks.
  • Input devices — analog and digital sensors, keypads and switches that supply data to the system.
  • Output devices — actuators, buzzers and display devices through which the system acts on the world.
  • Communication devices — Bluetooth, ZigBee or Wi-Fi modules that link the system to other systems.
  • User interface — application-specific controls for the operator.

Purposes

Data collection, storage and representation · data communication · data or signal processing · monitoring · controlling · application specific user interface.

Characteristics

Sophisticated functionality with real-time operation · low manufacturing cost and low power consumption · an application-dependent rather than general purpose processor · restricted memory and fewer system resources · dedicated to specific tasks · often operating under extreme environmental conditions, where software failure is far more severe than on a desktop.

Application domains

Home appliances, consumer electronics, automotive, health care, industrial, avionics, banking and communications.

Q1.2   Type C  ·  10 marks

Differentiate a general purpose computing system from an embedded system, with examples

Model answer

(Reproduce the six-row slide-13 table in full, then close with the paragraph below.)

BasisGeneral purposeEmbedded
Hardware and OSGeneric hardware + GPOS, runs many applicationsSpecial purpose hardware + embedded OS, one application set
Operating systemAlways presentMay or may not be present
User modificationApplications can be changed by the userFirmware is pre-programmed and non-modifiable
Deciding factorPerformance — faster is betterPerformance, power, memory and cost together
DeterminismNot requiredRequired for hard real-time systems
ExamplesPersonal computer, laptopDVD player, digital camera

Conclusion: the essential difference is generality versus specialisation. A general purpose system is optimised for the widest range of unknown future workloads; an embedded system is optimised for one known workload under fixed constraints of cost, power and size. That is why a desktop chases raw speed while an embedded designer will accept a slower processor that meets the deadline at a fraction of the power.

Q1.3   Type S  ·  10 marks

Classify and analyse: which of these are embedded systems?

For each of the following, state whether it is an embedded system and justify: (i) a washing machine, (ii) a laptop computer, (iii) a pacemaker, (iv) a smartphone, (v) an ATM.

Model answer
SystemVerdictJustification
(i) Washing machineYesDedicated firmware controlling motor, valves and timing; user cannot modify the program; purpose is controlling
(ii) LaptopNoGeneric hardware with a GPOS running arbitrary user applications; performance is the deciding factor
(iii) PacemakerYes — hard real-timeDeterministic execution is mandatory; a missed deadline is fatal. Extreme reliability and very low power
(iv) SmartphoneBorderline — a fourth-generation embedded systemThe deck classes smartphones as fourth generation: SoC and multicore processors with a high-performance RTOS. It runs user-installable applications like a GPOS, yet the hardware is special-purpose and highly integrated
(v) ATMYesSpecial purpose hardware — card reader, PIN pad, cryptoprocessor, dispenser — with fixed firmware; purpose is application specific user interface plus data communication
The reasoning to show

Apply three tests to any candidate: (1) is the hardware special-purpose or generic? (2) can the end user change the program? (3) is it dedicated to a specific function within a larger system? The smartphone is the interesting case precisely because it answers the three tests inconsistently — say so rather than forcing a yes or no.

Q1.4   Type S  ·  10 marks

Analyse an automatic washing machine as an embedded system

Draw the block diagram of an automatic washing machine, identify its input devices, output devices, control unit and communication interfaces, and state which of the six embedded system purposes it serves.

Model answer
BlockElements
Input devicesWater level sensor (analog), load/weight sensor (analog), door interlock switch (digital), keypad and mode selector
Control unitAn 8-bit or 16-bit microcontroller — the task is sequencing and threshold comparison, not computation
Output devicesInlet and drain solenoid valves via relays, drum motor under PWM control, heater relay, LCD display, buzzer
CommunicationOptional Wi-Fi module in smart models for remote start and cycle notification

Purposes served: primarily controlling (motor, valves, heater) and monitoring (water level, load, door state), with an application specific user interface (keypad and display). Smart models add data communication.

Why it is an embedded system: special purpose hardware, firmware fixed at manufacture and non-modifiable by the user, dedicated to one function, cost- and power-sensitive, and it must meet timing constraints such as closing the drain valve before the drum spins.

Q1.5   Type S  ·  5 marks

Match each system to its primary purpose

State the primary purpose (from the six on slide 11) of: a digital thermometer, a Wi-Fi router, an anti-lock braking system, a CCTV recorder, and a hearing aid.

Model answer
SystemPrimary purposeSecondary
Digital thermometerMonitoringData representation on the display
Wi-Fi routerData communicationData processing for packet routing
Anti-lock braking systemControllingMonitoring wheel speed; hard real-time
CCTV recorderData collection / storageSignal processing for compression
Hearing aidData (signal) processingExtreme low power, restricted memory

The pattern worth stating: most real systems serve two purposes — one primary and one supporting. Naming both shows you understand the classification rather than pattern-matching a keyword.

Q1.6   Type T  ·  5 marks

Why is software failure more severe in an embedded system than on a desktop?

Model answer
  1. No user to intervene. A desktop user reboots a hung application; an embedded system in a pacemaker, an aircraft or an unattended pump has nobody present. This is why a watchdog timer exists.
  2. Failure is physical, not just informational. A crashed spreadsheet loses data; a crashed airbag controller costs a life. Consequences leave the digital domain.
  3. Firmware is non-modifiable by the end user — a defect cannot be patched by the operator, and in mass-produced goods a field update may be impossible.
  4. Determinism is a requirement, not a preference. In a hard real-time system a late correct answer is a wrong answer.
  5. Fewer resources to detect and contain faults — no MMU on small parts, so a stray pointer corrupts arbitrary memory with no protection.

Design consequences to name: watchdog timers, safe-state initialisation on reset, redundancy in safety-critical designs, and extensive validation before manufacture — because there is no second chance.

UNIT 02

Classification of Embedded Systems

Module 1 · slides 18–27  ·  Types: T, C, S  ·  Weight: medium-high  ·  Four independent classification bases

The four bases (slide 19)

These four are independent. One system is classified on all four at once — a modern car ECU is fourth generation, large scale, deterministic hard real-time, and event triggered.

1 — By generation (slides 20–22)

GenerationProcessorCharacteristicsExamples
First4-bit and 8-bit — 8085, Z80Simple hardware and firmware developed in assemblyDigital telephone keypads, calculators
Second8-bit and 16-bitComplex and powerful instruction setData acquisition systems, SCADA
Third16-bit and 32-bitApplication-specific processors DSP and ASIC introduced; complex instruction set with pipelining; dedicated embedded real-time OS entered the marketRobotics, industrial process control, networking
FourthSoC, reconfigurable, multicoreHigh performance, tight integration and miniaturisation; high performance RTOSSmartphones, PDAs
The three markers that identify a generation

Bit width · what software is written in · whether an OS is present. First generation has no OS and assembly firmware; third generation is where the RTOS arrives; fourth generation is SoC and multicore. Quote the example devices — they are the quickest way to prove you know the boundary.

2 — By complexity and system performance (slides 23–25)

ScaleProcessorCharacteristicsExamples
Small-scaleLow cost, low performance 8 or 16-bit µP/µCSimple application needs; performance requirements not time criticalElectronic toys, digital multimeters
Medium-scaleMedium performance, low cost 16/32-bitSlightly complex hardware and software; usually contains an embedded operating systemDVD players, network routers
Large-scaleHigh performance 32 or 64-bit, SoC, PLDs or multi-coreHighly complex; mission critical, demanding high performance; may contain a complex high-performance RTOSMissile navigation, MRI scanner, ABS

3 — By execution behaviour (slide 26)

Deterministic: real-time systems versus non-real-time systems.

Hard real-timeSoft real-timeNon real-time
Missed deadlineTotal system failureDegraded quality, still usefulNo consequence
DeterminismMandatoryDesirableNot required
ExamplesAirbag, missile guidance, pacemaker, ABSVideo streaming, ATM transaction, printerData logger, weather station display
The distinction examiners test

In a hard real-time system a late correct answer is a wrong answer. An airbag that fires 200 ms after the crash is not slightly worse — it is useless and dangerous. In a soft real-time system a late frame merely degrades quality. Use that sentence.

4 — By triggering mechanism (slide 26)

Event triggeredTime triggered
Activated byAn external event, usually an interruptA fixed clock schedule
TimingUnpredictable arrivalFully predictable
SuitsRare, urgent eventsPeriodic sampling and control loops
ExamplesAirbag on impact, doorbell, emergency stopTemperature sampled every second, PID control loop

Approaches to building an embedded system (slide 27)

GPPASIPASIC
PerformanceLowHighVery high
FlexibilityExcellentGoodPoor
Hardware design effortNoneLargeVery large
Software design effortSmallLargeNone
PowerLargeMediumSmall
ReuseExcellentGoodPoor
MarketVery largeRelatively largeSmall
Cost driverMainly softwareSoCVolume sensitive

Theory and situation questions

Q2.1   Type T  ·  10 marks

Explain the classification of embedded systems with examples

Model answer

Introduction. Embedded systems are classified on four independent bases: generation, complexity and system performance, execution behaviour, and triggering mechanism. A single system is classified on all four simultaneously.

(Draw the slide-19 tree, then present each of the four tables above.)

Worked classification

An anti-lock braking system is: fourth generation (32-bit SoC with an RTOS), large scale (mission critical, high performance), hard real-time deterministic (a missed deadline causes loss of braking control), and event triggered (activated by wheel-lock detection).

Ending with one worked classification across all four bases is what turns a list into an answer.

Q2.2   Type S  ·  10 marks

Classify five given systems on all four bases

Classify each of the following by generation, scale, execution behaviour and triggering: (i) a pocket calculator, (ii) a network router, (iii) a cardiac pacemaker, (iv) a smart thermostat, (v) an MRI scanner.

Model answer
SystemGenerationScaleExecutionTriggering
Pocket calculatorFirstSmallNon real-timeEvent (keypress)
Network routerThirdMediumSoft real-timeEvent (packet arrival)
Cardiac pacemakerThird / fourthLarge (mission critical)Hard real-timeTime triggered, with event override
Smart thermostatFourthMediumSoft real-timeTime triggered (periodic sampling)
MRI scannerFourthLargeHard real-timeTime triggered sequence
How to justify each column

Generation — judge by bit width, whether an OS is present, and whether it uses SoC or multicore. Scale — judge by whether it is mission critical and by processor class. Execution — ask what happens if a deadline is missed. Triggering — ask whether the system waits for the world or works to a clock.

The pacemaker is the instructive one: it paces on a timed schedule but must respond immediately to a sensed natural beat, so it is time triggered with event override — a genuinely hybrid case worth pointing out.

Q2.3   Type C  ·  10 marks

Compare GPP, ASIP and ASIC as approaches to building an embedded system, and recommend one for two given products

Recommend an approach for (i) a high-volume smart electricity meter and (ii) a prototype robotics controller, justifying each.

Model answer

(Reproduce the eight-row slide-27 table, then answer the two cases.)

The trade-off in one sentence: moving from GPP to ASIC buys performance and power efficiency at the cost of flexibility and non-recurring engineering expense.

(i) High-volume smart electricity meter — ASIC (or a highly integrated SoC). The function is fixed for the product's life, so flexibility has no value. Volume is large enough that the high NRE cost is amortised into a very low per-unit cost. The meter runs continuously for years, so the ASIC's low power matters. Its very high performance is a bonus rather than the deciding factor.

(ii) Prototype robotics controller — GPP (a microcontroller such as an ATmega328P or an ARM Cortex-M). Requirements will change repeatedly during development, so flexibility dominates. Volume is one unit, so per-unit cost is irrelevant and NRE must be near zero. An FPGA is the reasonable middle answer if the prototype needs custom high-speed logic, because it is reconfigurable with no NRE.

The general rule to state

NRE cost is paid once and divided by the volume; unit cost is paid every time. High volume justifies high NRE; low volume never does. That single sentence answers every "which technology" question in this course.

Q2.4   Type S  ·  10 marks

Hard, soft or non real-time?

For each system, state whether it is hard real-time, soft real-time or non real-time, and describe the consequence of a missed deadline: (i) an airbag controller, (ii) a video streaming decoder, (iii) a weather data logger, (iv) an industrial robot arm, (v) an ATM cash dispenser.

Model answer
SystemClassConsequence of a missed deadline
Airbag controllerHardThe bag deploys after the occupant has already struck the wheel — total failure, and the late deployment is itself dangerous
Video streaming decoderSoftA dropped or stuttering frame; quality degrades but the system remains useful
Weather data loggerNonA sample is timestamped slightly late; no practical consequence
Industrial robot armHardThe arm overshoots its trajectory — collision, damage to workpiece or injury
ATM cash dispenserSoftThe transaction feels slow; correctness is preserved because the dispense is confirmed before completion

The test to apply: ask "is a late answer merely worse, or is it wrong?" If late means wrong, the system is hard real-time. If late means worse but still useful, it is soft. If lateness is invisible to the user, it is non real-time.

Design consequence: hard real-time systems require a deterministic processor with predictable interrupt latency, an RTOS with guaranteed scheduling, and a watchdog. Soft real-time systems can tolerate a general purpose OS with best-effort scheduling.

Q2.5   Type S  ·  10 marks

Event triggered or time triggered?

You are designing (i) a fire alarm, (ii) an air quality monitor logging every 15 minutes, (iii) a lift call system, and (iv) an engine management PID loop. Choose event- or time-triggered for each and justify. Then explain the consequences of choosing wrongly.

Model answer
SystemChoiceJustification
Fire alarmEvent triggeredFire is rare and urgent. Polling wastes power for years and risks a delayed response; an interrupt reacts in microseconds
Air quality monitorTime triggeredThe quantity changes slowly and the requirement is a regular record. A fixed 15-minute schedule gives uniform data and allows deep sleep between samples
Lift call systemEvent triggeredCalls arrive unpredictably; the system must respond to button presses whenever they occur
Engine management PID loopTime triggeredPID mathematics assumes a fixed sample interval. A varying interval corrupts the integral and derivative terms and destabilises the control
The consequences of choosing wrongly

Time-triggering an urgent event — polling a fire sensor once a minute means up to 60 seconds of undetected fire, and the processor never sleeps, so battery life collapses.

Event-triggering a control loop — a PID whose sample interval jitters produces wrong derivative and integral terms, so the loop oscillates or drifts. The PID case is the strongest example, because the mathematics itself depends on a constant interval.

Hybrid designs are normal: a system can be time triggered for routine sampling with an event-triggered interrupt for emergencies — which is exactly what a pacemaker does.

Q2.6   Type S  ·  10 marks

Scale selection for a product family

A company makes three products: a digital kitchen timer, a home network router, and a hospital ventilator. Classify each by scale, recommend a processor class and state whether an operating system is required.

Model answer
ProductScaleProcessor classOS required?Reason
Digital kitchen timerSmallLow cost 8-bit µCNoSimple needs, not time critical; a bare-metal loop suffices and an OS would add cost with no benefit
Home network routerMedium16/32-bit, medium performanceYes — embedded OSNeeds a TCP/IP stack, file system and concurrent connections; the deck lists routers as a medium-scale example that "usually contains an embedded operating system"
Hospital ventilatorLarge32-bit, high performance, possibly redundantYes — high performance RTOSMission critical and hard real-time; scheduling guarantees, watchdog and fault detection are mandatory

The progression to name: as scale rises, bit width rises, an OS appears, and the OS becomes a real-time OS. That is precisely the boundary between the deck's small, medium and large scale definitions.

The cost argument to close with: putting an RTOS in the kitchen timer would raise unit cost and memory requirements for no functional gain, in a product where cost is the deciding factor. Omitting one from the ventilator would make its timing guarantees unprovable. Matching the scale of the solution to the scale of the problem is the whole skill being tested.

UNIT 03

The Embedded System Design Process

Module 1 · slides 28–40  ·  Types: T, C, S, D  ·  Weight: highest  ·  Contains CAT-1 Q2

Top-down and bottom-up (slide 29)

Slide 29, quotable

Top-down — "From description of the system to concrete details."
Bottom-up — "Start with components to build a system."

Your CAT question says "use the top-down embedded system design approach", so you must show the flow proceeding downward from requirements to integration.

The five stages

The three goals to be considered (slide 30): manufacturing cost, performance, power consumption.

Tasks performed at each step (slide 30):

  • Analyze the design at each step — does it meet the specification?
  • Refine the design — add details.
  • Verify the design — does it meet the system goals?

Stage 1 — Requirements (slides 31–32)

Informal descriptions gathered from the customer are known as requirements. They are refined into a specification to begin designing the system architecture.

TypeDefinitionExamples
FunctionalNeeded output as a function of inputDisplay current latitude and longitude; open the door if temperature is normal
Non-functionalPerformance, cost, physical size, weight, power consumptionUpdate within 0.25 s; cost 30 USD; 250 grams; 100 mW

The deck's GPS requirements table (slide 32) is the template for any requirements table — reproduce its row headings:

RowGPS navigation system example
Product nameGPS Navigation System
PurposeConsumer grade moving map for driving use
InputsPower button, two control buttons
OutputsBack-lit LCD display 400×600
FunctionsFive-receiver GPS system; three user-selectable resolutions; always displays current latitude and longitude
PerformanceUpdates screen within 0.25 seconds upon movement
Power100 mW
Cost30 USD
Size and weight2" × 6" and 250 grams
Use these eight row headings in every design answer

Product name · Purpose · Inputs · Outputs · Functions · Performance · Power · Cost · Size and weight. Filling this table for the product in the question is the fastest way to produce a complete, marked requirements section.

Stage 2 — Specification (slides 33–34)

  • Requirements gathered are refined into a specification.
  • The specification serves as the contract between the customers and the architects.
  • It is essential to create working systems with a minimum of designer effort.
  • It must be specific, understandable and accurately reflect the customer's requirements.

The distinction to state: a requirement is informal and comes from the customer ("it should be accurate"); a specification is measurable and binding ("resolution 1 g over 0–5 kg").

Stage 3 — Architecture (slides 35–37)

  • The specification describes only the functions of the system.
  • The implementation of the system is described by the architecture.
  • The architecture is a plan for the overall structure, used later to design the components.
  • The system block diagram may be refined into two block diagrams — hardware and software.

Stage 4 — Hardware and software components (slides 38–39)

  • The architectural description specifies what components we need.
  • The component design effort builds them in conformance to the architecture and specification.
  • Includes both hardware and software modules.
  • Some components will be ready-made — CPU, memory chips.
  • In the moving map example, the GPS receiver is a predesigned standard hardware component and the topographic software a standard software module; the printed circuit board is what must be designed.
  • Embedded software must run properly in real time and not take more memory space than allowed.

Stage 5 — System integration (slide 40)

  • After the components are built, they are integrated.
  • Bugs are typically found during system integration.
  • By debugging a few modules at a time, simple bugs can be discovered.
  • By fixing the simple bugs early, more complex bugs can be discovered.
  • Appropriate debugging facilities designed in ease system integration problems.

Theory, comparison and design questions

PYQ   CAT-1 Q2  ·  Type D  ·  10 marks

Top-down design of an electronic weighing machine

Use the top-down embedded system design approach to design an Electronic Weighing machine. Choose the appropriate microcontroller, memory and components for your application and justify your choice.

Model answer — full exam format

Suggested mark split: design flow diagram 2 · requirements and specification 2 · architecture diagram 2 · component table 3 · justification 1.

Introduction

An electronic weighing machine converts the mechanical force of a load into an electrical signal, digitises it, converts the digital count into a calibrated mass, and displays the result. It is a small-scale embedded system: dedicated to a single function, cost-sensitive, battery-powered and with modest computational demand.

Top-down design flow

The top-down approach proceeds from an abstract description of the system to concrete details, analysing, refining and verifying the design at every step.

Step 1 — System requirements

Functional: measure the mass placed on the platform; display it digitally; provide a tare (zero) function; retain calibration data across power-off.

Non-functional: low unit cost; low power for battery operation; compact size; adequate accuracy; simple user interface.

Step 2 — Functional specification

ParameterSpecification
Measurement range0–5 kg
Resolution1 g
Display update rateTwice per second
TareSingle push button, zeroes the current reading
Supply5 V from a rechargeable battery pack
CalibrationScale factor and tare offset retained in non-volatile memory

Step 3 — Hardware / software architecture

Step 4 — Component selection

ComponentChoiceJustification
SensorLoad cell (strain gauge)Accurate conversion of mechanical force into an electrical signal
ADCHX71124-bit ADC designed specifically for load-cell applications, with an integrated low-noise programmable gain amplifier
MicrocontrollerATmega328PLow cost, low power, and sufficient GPIO and processing capability
Program memory32 KB FlashStores the embedded application firmware
RAM2 KB SRAMSufficient for temporary variables and calculations
Non-volatile memory1 KB EEPROMStores the calibration factor and tare data across power cycles
Display16×2 LCD or OLEDSimple and low-cost weight readout
InputTare push buttonZeroes the reading for container weight
PowerRechargeable battery with regulatorPortable operation at 5 V

Step 5 — Implementation, integration and testing, validation

Implementation: firmware reads the HX711 over its two-wire serial interface, applies the stored scale factor and tare offset, and drives the display. Integration and testing: each module is tested separately — sensor linearity, ADC communication, display — then combined and debugged a few modules at a time, so that simple bugs are found before complex ones. Validation: the assembled unit is checked against standard calibration weights across the full range, and battery life is measured.

Justification

The ATmega328P is sufficient because the weighing operation requires only moderate computation, low power and a small number of peripherals. The HX711 provides much better load-cell measurement resolution than the internal ADC of the microcontroller.

Make the ADC argument quantitative — this is the mark that separates answers

A typical load cell has a sensitivity of about 2 mV per volt of excitation, so at 5 V it produces roughly 10 mV at full scale. The ATmega328P's internal 10-bit ADC has a resolution of 5/1024 = 4.88 mV per step. The entire 5 kg range would therefore span about two ADC counts — completely unusable. The HX711's 24-bit converter with its 128× gain amplifier resolves that same signal into millions of counts, which is why an external ADC here is not a luxury but a necessity.

Q3.1   Type T  ·  10 marks

Explain the embedded system design process with a neat diagram

Model answer

Introduction. The embedded system design process proceeds from an abstract description of the system to concrete implementation details. The major goals to be considered throughout are manufacturing cost, performance and power consumption. At every step the designer must analyse the design against the specification, refine it by adding detail, and verify it against the system goals.

(Draw the five-stage flow diagram.)

The five stages

  1. Requirements — informal descriptions gathered from the customer. They may be functional (needed output as a function of input) or non-functional (performance, cost, physical size, weight, power consumption).
  2. Specification — the requirements refined into a precise, measurable form. It serves as the contract between the customers and the architects and must be specific, understandable and an accurate reflection of the customer's requirements.
  3. Architecture — the specification describes only what the system does; the architecture describes how it is implemented. It is the plan for the overall structure, and the system block diagram may be refined into separate hardware and software block diagrams.
  4. Hardware and software components — built in conformance to the architecture and specification. Some components are ready-made, such as the CPU and memory chips; others must be designed. Embedded software must run correctly in real time and stay within the allowed memory.
  5. System integration — components are combined. Bugs are typically found here. By debugging a few modules at a time, simple bugs are discovered, and fixing them early exposes the more complex ones. Debugging facilities designed into the system ease this stage.

Conclusion. The process is iterative: verification at any stage may send the designer back to refine an earlier one.

Q3.2   Type C  ·  10 marks

Compare top-down and bottom-up design approaches

Model answer
BasisTop-downBottom-up
DefinitionFrom description of the system to concrete detailsStart with components to build a system
Starting pointCustomer requirementsAvailable hardware and software modules
DirectionAbstract → concreteConcrete → abstract
StrengthThe design is driven by what the customer actually needsExploits existing, proven components; faster to prototype
WeaknessMay specify something no available component can deliverThe final system may not match the customer's requirement
SuitsNew products with clear requirementsProducts assembled from an existing platform or module library

In practice both are used together. A designer works top-down from requirements while simultaneously checking bottom-up whether components exist that can meet them — the deck notes that some components such as the CPU and memory chips are ready-made, which is inherently a bottom-up constraint on a top-down design.

Why your CAT question specified top-down: it wants to see you begin from requirements and derive the components, rather than starting with an Arduino and working out what it could measure. If a question says "top-down", the requirements section must come first and must be visible.

Q3.3   Type D  ·  10 marks

Top-down design of a smart irrigation system

Use the top-down approach to design an automatic smart irrigation system for a farm. It must sense soil moisture, switch a water pump on when the soil is dry and stop it when adequate moisture is reached. Choose the microcontroller, memory and components, and justify.

Model answer

Requirements

Functional: continuously sense soil moisture; switch the pump on below a dry threshold and off above a wet threshold; display moisture percentage and pump status; retain the threshold settings across power-off.
Non-functional: low cost, outdoor operation, low power, reliable unattended running.

Specification

Moisture range 0–100 %; sampling once per minute; dry threshold 30 %, wet threshold 60 % — a hysteresis band so the pump does not chatter at the setpoint; pump switched through a relay rated for the motor current; 5 V logic supply.

Architecture

Component selection

ComponentChoiceJustification
SensorResistive or capacitive soil moisture probeOutputs an analog voltage proportional to soil water content
ADCInternal 10-bit ADC of the ATmega328PThe sensor swings across the full 0–5 V range, so 4.88 mV resolution is more than adequate — no external ADC needed
MicrocontrollerATmega328PLow cost, low power, sufficient GPIO; the task is a simple threshold comparison
Program memory32 KB FlashStores the control firmware
RAM2 KB SRAMHolds sensor readings and averaging buffers
Non-volatile memory1 KB EEPROMRetains user-set thresholds across power cuts, which are common in farm settings
Actuator interfaceRelay module with optocouplerA pump draws far more than the 40 mA per-pin limit, so it must be switched, not driven
Display16×2 LCDLow-cost local readout of moisture and pump status

Justification

The ATmega328P is sufficient because the application performs a single threshold comparison at a very low sample rate and drives only one actuator; no floating-point mathematics, high clock speed or operating system is required.

Why this question is worth practising

It is the same template as CAT Q2 but reaches the opposite conclusion about the ADC. If you can argue both "external ADC needed" and "internal ADC sufficient" from the signal amplitude, you have genuinely understood the criterion rather than memorised one answer.

Q3.4   Type D  ·  10 marks

Top-down design of a digital blood pressure monitor

Design a home digital blood pressure monitor using the top-down approach. Choose the microcontroller, memory, sensors and actuators, and justify your choices.

Model answer

Requirements

Functional: inflate a cuff to a preset pressure; deflate slowly while sampling pressure; detect oscillometric pulses; compute systolic, diastolic and pulse rate; display the results; store the last 30 readings.
Non-functional: battery powered, portable, low cost, medically acceptable accuracy, simple one-button operation.

Specification

ParameterSpecification
Pressure range0–300 mmHg
Accuracy± 3 mmHg
Sampling rate≥ 100 Hz during deflation, to resolve pulse oscillations
Memory30 readings retained without power
Supply4 × AA cells, ≥ 300 measurements per set

Architecture

Component selection

ComponentChoiceJustification
SensorPiezoresistive pressure sensor with instrumentation amplifierConverts cuff pressure into a voltage; the oscillometric pulse rides on it as a small AC component
ADC12-bit or higher, internal to the MCUThe pulse oscillation is a few mmHg on a 300 mmHg baseline — roughly 1 % of full scale. A 10-bit ADC gives only about 10 counts of pulse amplitude; 12-bit gives 40, which is workable
MicrocontrollerARM Cortex-M0+ or M3 classNeeds digital filtering of the oscillometric waveform, which is beyond comfortable 8-bit fixed-point work; also gives low-power sleep modes
Program memory64–128 KB FlashFiltering and the oscillometric algorithm are larger than a threshold comparison
RAM8–16 KB SRAMBuffers a full deflation waveform for post-processing
Non-volatileEEPROM or Flash regionStores 30 readings and the factory calibration constants
ActuatorsPump motor + solenoid valve, via transistor driversBoth exceed the per-pin current limit and must be switched

Justification

Unlike the weighing machine, an 8-bit ATmega328P is not sufficient here. The system must sample at over 100 Hz, buffer a whole waveform in RAM, and run digital filtering to extract a small oscillation from a large baseline — a task requiring more SRAM and more arithmetic throughput than 2 KB and 16 MHz provide. A Cortex-M class device supplies both, plus deep-sleep modes that preserve battery life between measurements.

The contrast worth stating explicitly

Weighing machine → 8-bit is enough, external ADC required. Blood pressure monitor → 8-bit is not enough, internal ADC is enough (if 12-bit). The two examples pull in opposite directions on both axes, which proves you are reasoning from the signal and the algorithm rather than reciting a default answer.

Q3.5   Type S  ·  10 marks

Write requirements and specification for a smart door lock

For an electronic door lock with keypad entry, write the requirements using the deck's row headings, then convert them into a functional specification. Explain the difference between the two documents.

Model answer

Requirements (informal, from the customer)

RowContent
Product nameElectronic keypad door lock
PurposeKeyless entry for a residential front door
Inputs4×4 keypad, internal release button, door position switch
OutputsMotorised deadbolt, status LEDs, buzzer
FunctionsVerify a user PIN; unlock on a match; lock automatically; allow the PIN to be changed; lock out after repeated failures
PerformanceUnlock within one second of the final digit
PowerBattery operated, at least one year of normal use
CostCompetitive with mechanical locks
Size and weightMust fit a standard door mortise

Specification (measurable, binding)

ParameterSpecification
PIN length4 to 8 digits, stored in EEPROM
Unlock latency≤ 800 ms from final keypress to bolt fully retracted
Auto-relock10 s after the door position switch reports closed
Lockout3 failed attempts → 30 s lockout; attempt count stored in EEPROM so it survives a power cycle
Battery life≥ 8000 operations from 4 × AA; quiescent current ≤ 30 µA in sleep
Operating temperature−10 °C to +50 °C

The difference between the two

Requirements are informal descriptions gathered from the customer. They express intent — "battery should last a long time" — and may be vague, incomplete or even contradictory.

The specification refines those requirements into precise, measurable statements and serves as the contract between the customer and the architects. It must be specific, understandable and accurately reflect the customer's requirements.

The test to apply

A specification line must be testable. "Long battery life" cannot be tested; "≥ 8000 operations from 4 × AA cells" can. If you cannot design a test that gives a pass or fail, you have written a requirement, not a specification.

Security point worth a mark: storing the failed-attempt count in EEPROM rather than RAM means an attacker cannot defeat the lockout by cutting power after two wrong guesses.

Q3.6   Type S  ·  5 marks

Why are bugs found during system integration, and how should integration be managed?

Model answer

Why bugs surface at integration. Individual modules are tested against their own assumptions. Integration is the first point at which those assumptions meet each other — mismatched data formats, timing races between modules, shared resources such as a timer or a bus claimed by two drivers, and total memory or CPU budgets exceeded only when everything runs together. None of these are visible while testing a module alone.

The deck's management strategy (slide 40):

  1. Debug a few modules at a time rather than integrating everything at once, so that simple bugs can be discovered.
  2. Fix the simple bugs early, because doing so allows more complex bugs to be discovered — a complex bug is often masked by a simple one.
  3. Design appropriate debugging facilities into the system from the start, which eases integration problems.

Practical debugging facilities to name: a serial diagnostic port, LED status indicators, a bootloader for firmware update, test points on the PCB, and an in-circuit debug header. These cost almost nothing at design time and are impossible to add once the board is manufactured.

UNIT 04

Design Challenges, Constraints and Metrics

Module 1 · slides 41–46  ·  Types: T, S  ·  Weight: high  ·  The ten metrics appear in almost every justification

Constraints in embedded systems (slide 41)

Embedded systems are far more tightly constrained than traditional software systems.

ConstraintWhat it forces
CostCannot use a high-end or fast processor; cannot have more memory — the processor footprint must be small
SizeSmall processor footprint; cooling requirements; the processor must take up little space
PerformanceMust still deliver, e.g. digital camera snap rate, mobile phone contact list search
PowerBattery products need optimised power-saving algorithms and operating modes. Program size and number of instructions affect the processor's energy consumption
Memory and speedLimited available system memory and processor speed
Reactive and real-timeAdaptive cruise control, radar missile detection

The design challenge (slides 42–43)

Slides 42–43, quotable

Obvious design goal: construct an implementation with the desired functionality.
Key design challenge: simultaneously optimise numerous design metrics.
Design metric: a measurable feature of a system's implementation.

An implementation consists of a software processor with an accompanying program, a connection of digital gates, or some combination of the two. The difficulty is not achieving the function — it is achieving it while many competing metrics are optimised at once.

The ten design metrics (slides 44–45)

MetricDefinition
Unit costThe monetary cost of manufacturing each copy of the system, excluding NRE cost
NRE costNon-Recurring Engineering cost — the monetary cost of designing the system. Once designed, any number of units can be manufactured without additional design cost
SizeThe physical space required — measured in bytes for software, and gates or transistors for hardware
PerformanceThe execution time or throughput of the system
PowerThe power consumed, which determines battery lifetime or the cooling requirements of the IC — more power means more heat
FlexibilityThe ability to change the functionality without incurring heavy NRE cost. Software is typically considered very flexible
Time-to-marketThe time required to design and manufacture the system to the point it can be sold
Time-to-prototypeThe time to build a working version, which may be bigger or more expensive than the final product, but verifies usefulness and correctness
CorrectnessOur confidence that the functionality is implemented correctly — checked throughout design, with test circuitry inserted to verify manufacture
SafetyThe probability that the system will not cause harm
The designer's dilemma (slide 46) — a quotable closing paragraph

To meet this optimisation challenge the designer must be comfortable with a variety of hardware and software implementation technologies and able to migrate from one technology to another to find the best implementation for a given application and constraints. "Thus, a designer cannot simply be a hardware expert or a software expert, as is commonly the case today; the designer must be an expert in both areas."

Theory and situation questions

Q4.1   Type T  ·  10 marks

Explain the design challenge in embedded systems and the design metrics involved

Model answer

The challenge. The obvious design goal is to construct an implementation with the desired functionality. The key design challenge, however, is to simultaneously optimise numerous design metrics. A design metric is a measurable feature of a system's implementation. An implementation consists of a software processor with an accompanying program, a connection of digital gates, or some combination of the two.

(Reproduce the ten-metric table.)

Why the metrics conflict

The metrics are not independent — improving one usually worsens another:

ImproveAt the cost of
PerformancePower and unit cost
Unit cost (via an ASIC)NRE cost and flexibility
Flexibility (via software)Performance and power
Time-to-marketCorrectness and unit cost
Safety (via redundancy)Unit cost and size

Conclusion. Because no single implementation optimises everything, the designer must be comfortable with a variety of hardware and software technologies and able to migrate between them. A designer cannot simply be a hardware expert or a software expert; the designer must be an expert in both areas.

Q4.2   Type S  ·  10 marks

NRE and unit cost analysis

A product can be built two ways. Option A: a microcontroller-based design with NRE cost ₹5,00,000 and unit cost ₹400. Option B: an ASIC design with NRE cost ₹40,00,000 and unit cost ₹120. Find the break-even volume, and recommend an option for production runs of 5,000 units and 5,00,000 units.

Model answer

Total cost model

Total cost = NRE + (unit cost × volume). Per-unit cost to the company = NRE/volume + unit cost.

Break-even volume

The two cases

VolumeOption A totalOption B totalChoose
5,000500,000 + 2,000,000 = ₹25,00,0004,000,000 + 600,000 = ₹46,00,000A — saves ₹21 lakh
5,00,000500,000 + 200,000,000 = ₹20.05 crore4,000,000 + 60,000,000 = ₹6.4 croreB — saves ₹13.6 crore

Per-unit cost to the company

VolumeOption AOption B
5,000₹500₹920
12,500₹440₹440 — break-even
5,00,000₹401₹128
The principle to state

NRE cost is paid once and divided by the volume; unit cost is paid every time. As volume rises, NRE per unit tends to zero and the unit cost dominates. That is exactly why the deck lists ASIC cost as "volume sensitive" and GPP cost as "mainly on software".

Non-cost factors to mention: Option A also wins on flexibility and time-to-market, which may justify choosing it even above break-even if the specification is still changing.

Q4.3   Type S  ·  10 marks

Which metrics dominate?

For each product, identify the two dominant design metrics and explain what the designer would sacrifice to achieve them: (i) a cardiac pacemaker, (ii) a disposable fitness tracker, (iii) a satellite control computer, (iv) a smartphone launched to beat a competitor.

Model answer
ProductDominant metricsSacrificed
Cardiac pacemakerSafety and powerUnit cost and performance. Redundancy and extensive verification raise cost; the processor is deliberately slow to extend a battery that cannot be replaced without surgery
Disposable fitness trackerUnit cost and sizePerformance, flexibility and correctness margin. A cheap fixed-function part with minimal memory; a rare wrong step count is tolerable
Satellite control computerCorrectness and safetyUnit cost, size and time-to-market. Radiation-hardened parts cost orders of magnitude more and are generations behind in performance, but cannot be repaired after launch
Smartphone beating a competitorTime-to-market and performanceNRE cost and some correctness. Enormous engineering spend is accepted to ship first, and known minor defects are shipped and patched later by software update
The reasoning method

Ask two questions of any product: what happens if it fails? (drives safety and correctness) and what is the volume and who pays? (drives unit cost versus NRE). The pacemaker and the fitness tracker both measure a body signal on a battery, yet sit at opposite extremes on every metric — because the answer to "what happens if it fails" is completely different.

The smartphone case illustrates the metric students most often forget: time-to-market. Shipping six months late into a competitive market can be worse than shipping an imperfect product, which is why software-updatable designs are chosen.

Q4.4   Type C  ·  5 marks

Distinguish time-to-market from time-to-prototype, and NRE cost from unit cost

Model answer
Time-to-prototypeTime-to-market
DefinitionTime to build a working versionTime to design and manufacture to the point the system can be sold
OutputMay be bigger or more expensive than the final productThe production article
PurposeVerify the system's usefulness and correctness and refine its functionalityGenerate revenue
Typical technologyFPGA, development board, breadboardASIC or a production PCB
NRE costUnit cost
DefinitionCost of designing the systemCost of manufacturing each copy, excluding NRE
PaidOnceEvery unit
Effect of volumeDivided across the volume, so per-unit share fallsUnchanged per unit
Dominates forLow-volume productsHigh-volume products

The link between the two pairs: a fast time-to-prototype usually means a flexible, high-NRE-free technology such as an FPGA or a development board, while a low time-to-market for a high-volume product usually justifies a large NRE spend on an ASIC. Prototyping optimises for learning; production optimises for cost.

Q4.5   Type S  ·  10 marks

Resolve a design conflict

A team is designing a battery-powered air quality monitor. Marketing wants a colour touchscreen and Wi-Fi; engineering says the battery must last six months. Analyse the conflict in terms of design metrics and propose a resolution.

Model answer

The conflict, stated in metrics

RequirementMetric it servesMetric it damages
Colour touchscreenApplication-specific user interface; time-to-market appealPower (backlight dominates), unit cost, size
Wi-Fi connectivityData communicationPower (radio transmit current), unit cost
Six-month batteryPowerConstrains both features above

This is precisely the deck's key design challenge: the functionality is easy; optimising several metrics simultaneously is the difficulty.

Proposed resolution — attack duty cycle, not features

  1. Replace the always-on colour screen with a low-power display that is only lit on demand. A monochrome or e-paper display consumes power only when it changes; a button or motion sensor wakes the backlight for ten seconds. The user still sees a display; the average power falls by orders of magnitude.
  2. Make Wi-Fi periodic rather than continuous. Air quality changes slowly, so the radio wakes every 15 minutes, transmits a batch, and returns to deep sleep. Radio energy is dominated by time spent transmitting, not by having the feature.
  3. Choose a processor with genuine deep-sleep modes and wake-on-interrupt, so the CPU is idle for almost the whole interval — this is a processor selection criterion, not a software afterthought.
  4. Sample the sensor on a time-triggered schedule rather than continuously.

Residual trade-offs to declare honestly

Unit cost still rises with the radio; data is delayed by up to 15 minutes; the display is less attractive than a colour touchscreen. The resolution is not to refuse the features but to change their duty cycle, because average power, not peak power, sets battery life.

The general lesson: when two metrics appear irreconcilable, look for a third variable — here, the fraction of time each subsystem is active — that lets both be satisfied.

Q4.6   Type T  ·  5 marks

Explain the constraints under which embedded systems are designed

Model answer

Embedded systems are much more tightly constrained than traditional software systems. The deck identifies five:

  1. Cost — cannot use a high-end or fast processor, and cannot include more memory. The processor footprint must be small.
  2. Size — the processor footprint must be small, cooling requirements are limited, and the processor must occupy little space.
  3. Performance — despite the above, the system must still deliver, such as the snap rate of a digital camera or a contact search in a mobile phone.
  4. Power — battery-powered products need optimised power-saving algorithms and operating modes. Software program size and the number of instructions directly affect the processor's energy consumption, and continuous operation limits permissible power dissipation.
  5. Reactive and real-time behaviour — systems such as adaptive cruise control and radar missile detection must respond to the environment within a deadline.

The point to close on: these constraints act together, not separately. A faster processor solves the performance constraint but violates cost, size and power at once — which is why the design challenge is described as simultaneous optimisation of numerous metrics rather than the satisfaction of any one.

UNIT 05

Case Study — Automatic Chocolate Vending Machine

Module 1 · slides 47–58  ·  Types: T, D, S  ·  Weight: high  ·  The design process worked end to end

Why this case study matters

It is the design process, demonstrated

The ACVM runs the five stages of Unit 3 over one product: requirements → specifications → architecture (split into hardware and software) → components → system integration. Any "design X using the top-down approach" question can be answered by substituting your product into this skeleton.

Requirements (slides 48–50)

RowContent
PurposeTo sell chocolate through an ACVM from which children can automatically purchase chocolates. Payment is by inserting coins into a coin slot.
InputsCoins of different denominations through a coin slot; user commands.
OutputsChocolate, and a signal to the system that subtracts the cost from the value of the amount collected; display of menus for GUIs, time and date, advertisements, welcome and thank-you messages.
FunctionsA child sends commands using a GUI consisting of an LCD display and keypad · inserts coins for the cost of the chocolate and the machine delivers it · if the coins are not inserted in reasonable time, all coins are refunded · if the amount is more, the excess is refunded along with the chocolate · coins collect inside in a collector channel so the owner can retrieve the money through GUI commands · a USB wireless modem enables communication through the Internet to the ACVM owner.

Design metrics (slide 50)

MetricValue
Power dissipationAs required by mechanical units, display units and the computer system
PerformanceOne chocolate in two minutes, and 256 chocolates before the next filling
Process deadlinesThe machine waits a maximum of 30 s for the coins, and should deliver the chocolate within 60 s
User interfacesGraphic LCD or touch screen; commands by children or the owner through fingers on keypad or touch screen
Engineering costUS$ 50,000 (assumed) — this is the NRE cost
Manufacturing costUS$ 1,000 (assumed) — this is the unit cost

Notice that the deck's metric table is exactly the ten design metrics of Unit 4 applied to one product — engineering cost is NRE, manufacturing cost is unit cost, and process deadlines are the real-time performance requirement.

Specifications (slides 51–52)

  • Alphanumeric keypad on the top of the machine, for child interaction when buying and for owner commands.
  • Three-line LCD display unit on the top, displaying menus, entered text, pictograms, welcome and thank-you messages, and time and date.
  • Coin insertion slot so the child can insert coins.
  • Delivery slot to collect the chocolate, and coins if refunded.
  • Internet connection port so the owner can interact with the ACVM remotely.

Components — hardware (slide 56)

ComponentDetail
Coin sortingACVM-specific hardware to sort coins of different denominations
Power supplyMains 220 V 50 Hz or 110 V 60 Hz; internal circuits driven at 5 V 50 mA for electronics and 12 V 2 A for mechanical systems
NetworkingA TCP/IP port
TimingA 1 s resolution timer obtained by programming the 8051 timer
MemoryFlash memory as part of ROM, and RAM for storing temporary variables and the stack
ProcessorMicrocontroller 8051 MX with 8 MB ROM for application codes

Components — software (slide 57)

TaskFunction
Task_ReadPortsWaits for the coins and acts according to the coins collected
Task_CollectWaits for coins equal to or greater than the cost until timeout, and acts accordingly
Task_DeliverWaits for Task_ReadPorts, delivers the chocolate, and decreases the coin amount after delivery
Task_RefundWaits for a refund event and calculates the refund amount
Task_ExcessRefundRefunds the excess amount
Task_DisplayWaits for a message and displays it accordingly
Why the software is split into six tasks — a point worth making

Each task waits for an event and does one job. This is task decomposition for a real-time system: separate concerns become separate tasks so each can be given its own priority and deadline, tested independently, and scheduled by an RTOS. It also directly supports the integration strategy of slide 40 — debugging a few modules at a time.

System integration — test and validation (slide 58)

  • All user commands must function correctly.
  • All graphic displays and menus should appear as per the program.
  • Each task should be tested with test inputs.
  • Tested for 60 users per hour.

Check the arithmetic: 60 users per hour is one user per minute, and the performance metric allows one chocolate in two minutes. The validation criterion is therefore twice as demanding as the design metric — a deliberate safety margin worth pointing out.

Theory, design and situation questions

Q5.1   Type D  ·  10 marks

Design an automatic chocolate vending machine using the embedded design process

Model answer

(Work the five stages in order, drawing the three architecture diagrams.)

1. Requirements

Reproduce the purpose, inputs, outputs and functions from the table above, then the design-metrics table with its two headline numbers: one chocolate in two minutes, 256 chocolates before refilling, and the process deadlines of 30 s to insert coins, 60 s to deliver.

2. Specifications

Alphanumeric keypad, three-line LCD, coin insertion slot, delivery slot, Internet connection port.

3. Architecture

(Draw the overall system diagram, then refine it into separate hardware and software block diagrams — slides 53, 54 and 55.)

4. Components

(Give the hardware table and the six-task software table.)

5. System integration

All user commands verified; all displays and menus checked against the program; each task tested with test inputs; the whole machine load-tested at 60 users per hour.

Justification of the processor choice

The 8051 MX is appropriate because the workload is sequencing and threshold comparison, not computation: read coin sensors, accumulate a value, compare against a price, drive a delivery mechanism and update a display. It provides the on-chip timer needed for the 1 s resolution deadline timing, sufficient I/O ports for the coin sorter, keypad, display and delivery mechanism, and it is low cost, which matters at a manufacturing cost target of US$ 1,000.

The 8 MB ROM is far larger than the control logic needs; it is required for the graphic menus, pictograms and advertisements listed in the outputs.

Q5.2   Type S  ·  10 marks

Adapt the ACVM design to an automatic coffee vending machine

The same manufacturer now wants a coffee machine offering three drink types at different prices, with cup dispensing, water heating and card payment. Restate the requirements, specifications and software tasks, and identify what must change in the hardware.

Model answer

Requirements — what changes

RowACVMCoffee machine
InputsCoins, user commandsCoins, card reader, user commands, water level and temperature sensors
OutputsChocolate, displayCup, three ingredient dispensers, hot water, display
FunctionsOne product, one priceThree products at three prices; heat water to a set temperature; dispense cup before liquid
PerformanceOne chocolate in 2 minutesOne cup in ~45 s once water is hot; water heated to 90 °C within 3 minutes from cold
Process deadlines30 s for coins, 60 s to deliver30 s for payment, 60 s to deliver, and the valve must close before the cup overflows — a hard real-time constraint the ACVM does not have

Software tasks — what changes

TaskStatus
Task_ReadPortsRetained, extended to read the card reader
Task_CollectRetained, must now compare against three prices
Task_DeliverSplit into Task_DispenseCup and Task_DispenseDrink, which must run in that order
Task_Refund / Task_ExcessRefundRetained for coin payment; not applicable to card
Task_DisplayRetained, extended for a product-selection menu
Task_HeatControlNew — closed-loop water temperature control, running continuously in the background
Task_CardTransactionNew — communicates with the payment gateway over the network port

Hardware changes

  • Analog inputs required — the ACVM needed only digital coin sensors; the coffee machine needs an ADC for the water temperature sensor.
  • Heater control — a high-current relay or triac, plus a safety thermal cut-out independent of the processor.
  • Card reader and secure element — payment data must be handled in a secure enclosure, as in the ATM case study of Unit 14.
  • More powerful processor — closed-loop temperature control plus a payment protocol stack exceeds a plain 8051; a 32-bit microcontroller with an ADC and a network stack is appropriate.
The insight the question is testing

Adding a heater turns a sequencing machine into a control system. The ACVM has no feedback loop at all — it counts coins and actuates. The coffee machine must hold a temperature, which introduces an analog sensor, a continuous background task and a safety hazard. That single change is what forces the processor upgrade.

Q5.3   Type S  ·  10 marks

Decompose a parking-ticket machine into software tasks

Following the ACVM's task model, decompose an automatic parking-ticket machine into software tasks. State what event each task waits for and assign each a priority and a deadline.

Model answer
TaskWaits forActionPriorityDeadline
Task_VehicleDetectLoop sensor or IR beamSignals that a vehicle is at the barrierHigh100 ms
Task_ReadPortsCoin, card or button inputAccumulates payment or a ticket requestMedium200 ms
Task_CollectPayment ≥ tariff, or timeoutConfirms payment; triggers refund on timeoutMedium30 s timeout
Task_PrintTicketTask_Collect confirmationPrints entry time, date and barcodeMedium5 s
Task_BarrierTicket taken, or valid exit ticketRaises the barrier; lowers after the vehicle clearsHighest500 ms — safety critical
Task_RefundRefund event or timeoutCalculates and returns coinsLow10 s
Task_DisplayA messageShows tariff, instructions, free spacesLow1 s
Task_SlotCountEntry or exit eventMaintains the free-space count, stored non-volatilelyLow2 s
Task_NetworkPeriodic timerReports occupancy and takings to the operatorLowestBest effort
The two principles to state

1. Priority follows consequence, not importance to the business. Task_Barrier is highest priority because lowering the barrier onto a vehicle causes physical harm — a safety deadline outranks a revenue deadline. Task_Network is lowest because a late report costs nothing.

2. Each task waits for exactly one event. That is the ACVM pattern from slide 57, and it is what allows tasks to be tested with test inputs individually, then integrated a few at a time.

Non-volatile requirement: the free-space count must survive a power cut, so it belongs in EEPROM — exactly the argument used for the weighing machine's calibration data.

Write a test and validation plan for the ACVM

Based on slide 58, expand the ACVM's four validation criteria into a full test plan covering functional, boundary, timing and failure cases.

Model answer
CategoryTestPass criterion
FunctionalInsert exact amountChocolate delivered, no refund, count decremented
Insert excess amountChocolate delivered and excess refunded
Owner retrieves collected coins via GUI commandCollector channel released, amount reported correctly

The category students always omit

Failure cases. The deck's four criteria cover functional and load testing only. A vending machine handles money, so the power-cut-mid-transaction case is the one that matters commercially: the design must record the transaction state in non-volatile memory before actuating the delivery mechanism, so that on restart it can complete or refund but never do both.

Link back to slide 40: each task is tested with test inputs individually first, and only then is the whole machine load-tested — debugging a few modules at a time so simple bugs are found before complex ones.

Q5.5   Type T  ·  5 marks

Why does the deck refine the ACVM system diagram into two separate diagrams?

Model answer

Slide 35 states that in the architecture stage "the system block diagram may be refined into two block diagrams — hardware and software", and slides 53–55 do exactly that for the ACVM.

Why the split is necessary

  1. They answer different questions. The hardware diagram answers what physical parts exist and how they connect; the software diagram answers what tasks exist and what events they wait for. A single diagram mixing coin sorters with task queues communicates neither clearly.
  2. They are built by different teams. The architecture is the plan used later to design the components, and hardware and software components are developed in parallel by different engineers.
  3. The hardware/software partition is itself a design decision. Deciding that coin sorting is done by ACVM-specific hardware rather than by software analysing a sensor waveform is an architectural choice, and drawing the two diagrams forces that decision to be made explicitly.
  4. It supports integration. Testing each software task with test inputs is possible only if the tasks are identified as separate entities in the architecture.

In an exam, drawing both diagrams where the question involves a non-trivial product demonstrates that you understand the architecture stage rather than just producing one picture.

Q5.6   Type S  ·  10 marks

Justify the ACVM's power supply and memory decisions

Explain why the ACVM uses two internal supply rails, and why it needs 8 MB of ROM when its control logic would fit in a few kilobytes.

Model answer

Two supply rails

The deck specifies 5 V at 50 mA for the electronics and 12 V at 2 A for the mechanical systems, derived from a 220 V 50 Hz or 110 V 60 Hz mains input.

  • The current ratio is 40:1. Solenoids, the coin sorter and the delivery mechanism draw amperes; digital logic draws milliamps. A single rail sized for the mechanics would be wasteful and would couple motor noise directly into the processor supply.
  • The voltage differs because solenoids and small motors are efficiently driven at 12 V, while the microcontroller requires a regulated 5 V.
  • Isolation. Switching an inductive load causes supply dips and spikes. Separate rails, with the mechanical ground returned separately, prevent those transients from resetting the microcontroller — the same reason the servo in a Module 2 design is powered from the rail and only signalled from a pin.

Why 8 MB of ROM

The control logic — counting coins, comparing against a price, actuating a delivery mechanism — would fit in a few kilobytes. The 8 MB is required by the outputs listed in the requirements: menus for GUIs, pictograms, advertisements, and welcome and thank-you messages, plus time and date rendering.

Graphics dominate memory, not logic. A single full-screen image on a graphic LCD can occupy tens of kilobytes; a library of advertisements and pictograms scales to megabytes. This is a general principle worth stating: in a product with a rich user interface, the memory requirement is set by the interface assets, not by the algorithm.

The design-metric link: this is size measured in bytes for software, one of the ten metrics, traded against unit cost — memory is a per-unit expense, so the 8 MB must be justified by the requirement rather than added speculatively.

The deck pairs µP with Von Neumann/RISC and µC with Harvard/CISC. Reproduce the table as given — it is what you are marked against. The security angle — this explains the "Protection" row of slide 59

In a Harvard machine, data memory is not executable and program memory is not writable at run time. A buffer overflow therefore cannot inject code that the CPU will execute. That is why the deck rates the microcontroller as having more protection than the microprocessor.
