Theory, comparison and situation questions

Q6.1   Type C  ·  10 marks

Differentiate a microprocessor from a microcontroller

Model answer

(Reproduce the eight-row slide-59 table, then add the paragraph below.)

The essential difference

A microprocessor is a CPU alone. Memory, I/O ports, timers and converters are external chips that the designer selects and connects — which is why the deck credits it with flexibility: "the designer can decide on the amount of ROM, RAM and I/O ports."

A microcontroller is a complete computer on one chip — CPU plus a fixed amount of ROM, RAM, I/O ports, timers and often ADC and serial interfaces. Nothing can be resized, but nothing needs to be added.

Why the other rows follow from that

RowWhy it follows
Design time (more vs less)A µP system needs a multi-chip board to be designed, laid out and debugged; a µC needs a power supply and a crystal
Cost (high vs low)One chip is cheaper than five, and a smaller PCB costs less
Power (high vs low)Driving signals across a board between chips consumes far more energy than on-die connections
Processing power (high vs low)The µP's external memory can be large and fast; the µC is limited to what fits on the die
Protection (less vs more)The µC's Harvard architecture keeps data memory non-executable

Selection rule: choose a microcontroller for a dedicated control application with modest memory needs — a washing machine, a weighing scale. Choose a microprocessor where computing power, large memory or an operating system is required — a router, a tablet, a data terminal.

Q6.2   Type T  ·  10 marks

Explain Von Neumann and Harvard architectures with neat diagrams

Model answer

(Draw both diagrams side by side, then give the comparison table.)

Von Neumann architecture

A single memory holds both program instructions and data, accessed over a single bus. The CPU therefore cannot fetch an instruction and read or write data in the same cycle — the two operations compete for the bus. This limitation is known as the Von Neumann bottleneck. Its advantage is simplicity and lower hardware cost, and memory can be freely allocated between program and data. Examples: 8085, 8086, and the ARM7.

Harvard architecture

Separate program and data memories, each with its own bus. The CPU can fetch the next instruction while simultaneously reading or writing data, so throughput is higher for the same clock rate. The program and data words may even have different widths — the PIC uses a 14-bit program word with 8-bit data. The cost is more silicon, more pins and more complex decoding, and memory cannot be reallocated between the two spaces. Examples: 8051, AVR, PIC.

Modified Harvard

Most modern processors, including ARM9 and the Cortex families, use a modified Harvard arrangement: separate instruction and data caches giving the speed benefit, over a unified main memory giving the flexibility of a single address space.

Security consequence

Because a Harvard machine cannot execute from data memory, injected code in a data buffer can never be run. This is one reason the deck rates microcontrollers as offering more protection than microprocessors.

Q6.3   Type S  ·  10 marks

Microprocessor or microcontroller?

For each system, choose a microprocessor or a microcontroller and justify: (i) a washing machine controller, (ii) a home Wi-Fi router, (iii) a digital weighing scale, (iv) a point-of-sale billing terminal with a printer and touchscreen, (v) a smoke detector.

Model answer
SystemChoiceJustification
Washing machine controllerµCDedicated sequencing and threshold logic; needs on-chip timers, ADC and I/O; cost-sensitive high volume; no OS required
Home Wi-Fi routerµP (or an SoC)Needs a TCP/IP stack, file system and concurrent connections, so an embedded OS and external DRAM and Flash are required — the fixed on-chip memory of a µC is insufficient
Digital weighing scaleµCThe CAT Q2 answer: moderate computation, low power, few peripherals; the ATmega328P is sufficient
POS billing terminalµP / application processorTouchscreen GUI, printer driver, network payment stack and large memory; the deck's spot billing machine case study chooses a 32-bit ARM Cortex-M3 with expandable 8–16 MB data memory
Smoke detectorµCExtremely cost- and power-sensitive; one sensor, one alarm; must run for years on a battery, which the µC's low power supports
The two questions that decide it

1. Does it need an operating system? If yes — a network stack, a file system, concurrent tasks — you need external memory and a microprocessor. 2. Does the fixed on-chip memory suffice? If the whole program and data fit in tens of kilobytes, a microcontroller wins on cost, power, size and design time.

The POS terminal is the boundary case: it is a control application, but its user interface, printer and payment protocol push its memory requirement past what a microcontroller offers — which is exactly why the deck's real-world example uses a Cortex-M3 with megabytes of external memory rather than an 8051.

Q6.4   Type C  ·  10 marks

Compare RISC and CISC, and explain which the ARM and the 8051 use

Model answer

(Reproduce the nine-row RISC/CISC table.)

ARM — RISC

ARM is the world's leading provider of RISC-based microprocessors. Its RISC nature shows in three deck-stated features: a load-store architecture (only load and store instructions access memory, all data processing is register to register), a uniform and fixed-length instruction set (32-bit ARM and 16-bit Thumb), and multiple-stage pipelined operation, which fixed-length instructions make straightforward.

8051 — CISC

The Intel MCS-51 is described as a Harvard architecture, complex instruction set computing (CISC) architecture single-chip microcontroller. Its instructions vary in length, many operate directly on memory or on individual bits, and most take multiple machine cycles — the comparison table on slide 123 lists the 8051 at 12 clocks per instruction cycle against ARM's 1 clock per instruction cycle.

The trade-off

RISC advantageCISC advantage
Faster — near one instruction per cycleHigher code density — fewer instructions for the same work
Easy pipelining and superscalar executionSimpler compilers
Simpler, smaller, lower-power siliconLess program memory required

Why ARM's Thumb mode exists: RISC's weakness is code density, and embedded systems have restricted memory. Thumb's 16-bit instruction encoding recovers most of the density of a CISC machine while keeping the RISC pipeline — which is why the deck lists "high performance and high code density" together as an ARM feature.

Q6.5   Type S  ·  5 marks

Why does a Harvard machine execute faster at the same clock speed?

Explain with reference to instruction fetch and data access, and state one situation where Von Neumann is preferable.

Model answer

The mechanism. Executing an instruction requires at minimum a fetch of the instruction and, for a load or store, an access to data. In a Von Neumann machine both travel over the same bus to the same memory, so they must be serialised — the CPU fetches, then accesses, taking two bus cycles. In a Harvard machine the program bus and data bus are independent, so the fetch of the next instruction happens in the same cycle as the data access of the current one. Throughput approximately doubles for memory-intensive code without any increase in clock rate.

This also makes pipelining far more effective: a pipeline stalls whenever two stages need the same bus, and separate buses remove that class of stall.

Where Von Neumann is preferable

  • Flexible memory allocation. With one memory, a program that is small but data-heavy, or large but data-light, uses the same total memory efficiently. A Harvard machine with 32 KB of program memory cannot lend any of it to data.
  • Lower cost and simpler hardware — one bus, fewer pins, simpler decoding.
  • Self-modifying code and program loading. Running an operating system that loads programs into memory requires writing to what will become instruction space, which pure Harvard forbids. This is why general purpose computers are Von Neumann and why modern processors use modified Harvard — separate caches over a unified memory — to get both benefits.
Q6.6   Type S  ·  10 marks

Architecture selection for a motor control unit

You must specify the processor for a three-phase motor drive that runs a control loop at 20 kHz, drives six PWM outputs, reads three current sensors and communicates over CAN. State the architecture features you require and justify each.

Model answer

What the application demands

RequirementArchitecture feature neededJustification
20 kHz control loop = 50 µs per iterationRISC core at ≥ 50 MHz with single-cycle executionAt 12 clocks per instruction (8051) only a few hundred instructions fit in 50 µs; at 1 clock per instruction thousands do
Simultaneous instruction fetch and sensor data accessHarvard or modified HarvardThe loop is memory-intensive; separate buses avoid serialising fetch and access
Six synchronised PWM outputsAdvanced timer with complementary outputs and dead-time insertionThree-phase inverters need paired high and low switches that must never conduct together
Three current sensors read at the PWM instantMulti-channel ADC with timer-triggered conversionCurrent must be sampled at a precise point in the PWM cycle; software triggering would jitter
Park and Clarke transforms, PI loopsHardware floating-point unit or a DSP instruction setTrigonometric and filter mathematics at 20 kHz is not feasible in 8-bit fixed point
CAN communicationOn-chip CAN controllerPeripheral set analysis — an external controller costs pins, board area and latency
SafetyWatchdog and fault-detection inputsA hung processor leaving both inverter switches on destroys the drive

Conclusion

These requirements exclude an 8-bit CISC microcontroller and point to a 32-bit RISC microcontroller with a modified Harvard architecture, an FPU, advanced motor-control timers and an integrated CAN controller — an ARM Cortex-M4 class device such as the STM32F4 used in the drone answer of Unit 11.

The reasoning pattern to reuse

Convert each functional requirement into an architectural feature, then justify the feature. That two-column table is the answer. It is the same method as the ten-row selection criteria table of Module 3, applied at the level of architecture rather than part number.

Theory, comparison and situation questions

Q7.1   Type T  ·  10 marks

Explain application-specific processors, with their benefits and drawbacks

Model answer

Definition

An application-specific instruction-set processor (ASIP) is designed for a particular class of applications sharing common characteristics — digital signal processing, telecommunications, embedded control. It is not a single-application device like an ASIC, nor a fully general processor.

How it is designed

The designer optimises the datapath for the application class, which involves two complementary moves: adding special functional units for operations that class performs constantly, and eliminating other infrequently used units. A DSP-oriented ASIP, for example, adds a single-cycle multiply-accumulate unit and hardware loop counters while removing complex addressing modes it will never use.

Classification of application-specific processors

TypeDomain
DSPReal-time signal processing — audio, video, communications
ASIPA domain with a customisable instruction set — crypto, vision, IoT
ASICCustom hardware for one fixed application
GPUMassively parallel vector and matrix operations

Benefits

Flexibility while still achieving good performance, power and size. Because it remains programmable, the same silicon serves a family of related products and can be updated in software — something an ASIC cannot do.

Drawbacks

Large NRE cost to build the processor itself, and to build a compiler for it if one does not already exist. Designing a processor is expensive; designing the toolchain that makes it usable is often more expensive still, and without a good compiler the performance advantage is unreachable.

Where it sits

Between the GPP and the ASIC on the deck's slide-27 spectrum: better performance and power than a GPP, more flexibility and lower NRE than an ASIC.

Q7.2   Type C  ·  10 marks

Compare ASIC, FPGA, CPLD, DSP, GPU and ASIP

Model answer

(Reproduce the slide-77 table. If time is short, give these six rows: definition, configurability, performance, power efficiency, cost per unit, best for.)

The decision tree to close with

Where ASIP fits: when the function is fixed for a domain rather than a single product, and the volume across that domain justifies designing a processor and its compiler.

Q7.3   Type S  ·  10 marks

How does processor choice differ between a smartphone and an automotive control system?

Model answer

(This is the deck's own slides 73–76. Reproduce the comparison table, then close with the paragraph below.)

Smartphone

Smartphones require versatile processors capable of handling diverse workloads — multimedia, communication and computation. The processors prioritise high performance, low power consumption and support for multiple applications. GPPs run the general purpose OS and multitasking applications, giving flexibility and easy updates. DSPs handle audio and video encoding, image processing and 4G/5G protocols. ASPs appear as dedicated GPU and NPU subsystems for gaming and AI.

Automotive control system

Automotive systems demand processors that emphasise real-time performance, safety and reliability over versatility. GPPs are used only in infotainment and non-critical control, because they lack the reliability and real-time performance required for safety-critical systems. DSPs are used in ADAS for radar and lidar processing. ASPs handle engine management, braking and sensor fusion, optimised for specific real-time control with reduced complexity and cost.

The underlying difference

A smartphone optimises for unknown future workloads; an automotive controller optimises for one known workload that must never fail.

ConsequenceSmartphoneAutomotive
DeterminismBest effort — a dropped frame is acceptableMandatory — a missed deadline is a hazard
UpdatabilityEssential; apps installed by the userRestricted; certified firmware
Lifetime2–3 years15+ years, so long-term part supply matters
EnvironmentRoom temperature, pocket−40 °C to +125 °C, vibration, EMI
Failure costRebootInjury or death
Q7.4   Type S  ·  10 marks

Select an implementation technology for four products

Recommend a technology and justify for: (i) a bitcoin mining accelerator produced in millions, (ii) a university research prototype for a new video codec, (iii) address decoding glue logic on a memory board, (iv) a real-time noise-cancelling headphone chip.

Model answer
ProductTechnologyJustification
(i) Bitcoin mining acceleratorASICThe hashing function is fixed and will never change, so flexibility has zero value. Volume is in the millions, so the high NRE is amortised to nothing. ASIC gives the highest performance and best power efficiency, and in mining, performance per watt is the product. Reconfigurability is explicitly not wanted
(ii) Video codec research prototypeFPGAThe algorithm will change repeatedly during research, so reconfigurability many times is essential. Volume is one or two units, so the high per-unit cost is irrelevant, while the absence of NRE is decisive — an ASIC respin would cost more than the entire project. Development time is short–medium
(iii) Address decoding glue logicCPLDThe logic is simple control/state-machine logic — exactly the deck's "best for" entry. Very short development time, low–moderate cost, low latency. An FPGA would be over-specified and a discrete-gate solution would occupy more board area
(iv) Noise-cancelling headphone chipDSP, or a DSP-class ASIPContinuous real-time signal processing with deterministic low latency — cancellation must be applied within a fraction of a millisecond or the phase is wrong. Good power efficiency for DSP tasks matters in a battery product. At very high volume this becomes an ASIP or ASIC with a DSP core, gaining efficiency once the algorithm is frozen
The two-question method

1. Will the function change? If yes → FPGA or a programmable processor. If no → ASIC becomes viable.
2. What is the volume? High volume justifies NRE; low volume never does.

Products (i) and (ii) are the same kind of computation — heavy parallel arithmetic — and land on opposite technologies purely because of volume and volatility. Making that point explicitly is what demonstrates understanding.

Q7.5   Type S  ·  10 marks

DSP or general purpose processor?

A team must implement a real-time FIR filter running 256 taps at 48 kHz. Compare implementing it on a general purpose microcontroller versus a DSP, with reasoning about the operation count.

Model answer

The computational load

On a general purpose microcontroller

An 8-bit CISC device at 12 clocks per instruction cannot approach this. Even a 16 MHz single-cycle RISC part executing a MAC in, optimistically, 5 instructions manages roughly 3.2 million MAC/s — four times too slow, before any other work. A GPP must also fetch each coefficient and sample separately, and lacks saturating arithmetic, so overflow must be handled in software.

On a DSP

A DSP is a specialised microprocessor for real-time signal processing whose datapath is optimised for exactly this. The relevant architectural features:

  • Single-cycle MAC unit — the multiply and the accumulate complete together, so one tap costs one cycle.
  • Harvard or multi-bus memory — the coefficient and the sample are fetched simultaneously, so the MAC is never starved.
  • Hardware zero-overhead loops — no branch or counter instruction per tap.
  • Circular addressing — the delay line advances without moving data in memory.
  • Saturating arithmetic — overflow clips instead of wrapping, which is the correct behaviour for audio.

A 100 MIPS DSP therefore delivers about 100 million MAC/s, giving roughly 8× headroom over the requirement.

Recommendation and trade-off

Use a DSP. It has low, deterministic latency and good power efficiency for DSP tasks, both essential in real-time audio. The costs are a moderate unit price, a specialised toolchain, and programmers who understand fixed-point arithmetic.

The general rule to state: when the inner loop is dominated by multiply-accumulate over streaming data, a DSP wins; when the workload is control flow and decisions, a GPP wins. That is precisely the deck's split between DSPs for "computation intensive applications such as image processing, communication devices, voice to text converter" and microcontrollers for "low-end to high-end control applications".

Q7.6   Type C  ·  5 marks

Why is an FPGA preferred over an ASIC for prototyping, despite its lower performance?

Model answer
FactorFPGAASIC
NRE costNoneVery high — mask sets and verification
ReconfigurableYes, many timesNo — a design error means a full respin
Development timeShort–mediumLong and costly
Time-to-prototypeDays to weeksMonths
Per-unit costHighVery low in mass production

The reasoning. During prototyping the design changes constantly. Every change in an ASIC requires a new mask set and months of turnaround, at a cost that can exceed the entire prototype budget. An FPGA is reprogrammed in minutes at zero marginal cost.

Two of the ten design metrics dominate here: time-to-prototype — the time to build a working version that verifies usefulness and correctness — and flexibility, the ability to change functionality without incurring heavy NRE cost. The FPGA's lower performance and higher per-unit cost are irrelevant when the volume is one and the purpose is learning.

The standard industrial path is therefore FPGA first, ASIC second: prototype and validate on the FPGA where changes are free, then migrate the proven design to an ASIC once the function is frozen and the volume justifies the NRE.

UNIT 08

The 8051 Microcontroller

Module 1 · slides 78–98  ·  Types: T, C, S  ·  Weight: high  ·  A likely alternative to the ARM question

Introduction (slide 79)

Slide 79, quotable

"The Intel MCS-51 (commonly termed 8051) is a Harvard architecture, complex instruction set computing (CISC) architecture, single chip microcontroller series developed by Intel in 1980 for use in embedded systems."

Intel's original MCS-51 family used NMOS technology; later versions identified by a letter C in their name (e.g. 80C51) used CMOS and consume less power.

Features (slide 80)

FeatureValue
CPU8-bit
On-chip program memory (ROM)64K bytes addressable — see the errata note below

Errata — the decks contradict each other

Slide 80 states "64K bytes on-chip program memory (ROM)"; slide 93 states the 8051 "has 4K of Code Memory... that is it has 4KB ROM and RAM of 128 bytes". Slide 93 is correct. The standard 8051 has 4 KB of internal ROM and can address up to 64 KB of external program memory through its 16-bit address bus. Write it that way — the 64 K figure is the addressing limit, not the on-chip size.

The blocks explained (slides 91–98)

BlockFunction (deck wording)
CPUThe brain of the microcontroller. It monitors and controls all operations. The user has no direct control over the CPU's work. It reads the program written in ROM, executes it and performs the expected task
Interrupt controlFive interrupt sources: two external (INT0, INT1), two timer (TF0, TF1) and one serial port (RI/TI). The 8051 can be configured to temporarily terminate or pause the main program on an interrupt; when the subroutine completes, the main program resumes
ROM (program memory)Stores the program — 4 KB of code memory
RAM (data memory)Stores data or operands temporarily — 128 bytes
Bus controlControls the operation of the address and data bus. A bus is a collection of wires acting as a communication channel. Address bus: 16-bit, used to address memory locations. Data bus: 8-bit, used to carry data
Crystal oscillatorThe microcontroller is a digital circuit device and requires a clock. The oscillator's stable output pulses enable synchronised work of all parts
I/O portsFour ports of 8 bits each, configurable as input (1) or output (0) depending on logic state, giving 32 I/O pins for peripherals
Timers/countersTwo 16-bit timer/counters, usable to generate a time delay or to count events happening outside. Since the 8051 has an 8-bit architecture, each 16-bit timer is accessed as two separate registers — low byte and high byte
Serial portOne UART, full duplex so it can transmit and receive simultaneously. P3.0 = RXD, P3.1 = TXD. Programmable for four different modes and a range of frequencies

Theory, comparison and situation questions

Q8.1   Type T  ·  10 marks

Describe the architecture of the 8051 microcontroller with a neat block diagram and explain its key features

Model answer

Introduction

The Intel MCS-51, commonly termed the 8051, is a Harvard architecture, CISC, single-chip microcontroller series developed by Intel in 1980 for use in embedded systems. The original family used NMOS technology; later CMOS versions such as the 80C51 consume less power.

Block diagram

Explanation of the blocks

(Give the nine-row block table above — CPU, interrupt control, ROM, RAM, bus control, oscillator, I/O ports, timers, serial port.)

Key features

(Give the eleven-row features table. State 4 KB on-chip ROM, expandable to 64 KB externally.)

Applications

Home appliances, industrial control, automotive subsystems, vending machines — the deck's own ACVM case study uses an 8051 MX — and any low-cost dedicated control application.

Q8.2   Type T  ·  10 marks

Explain the interrupt structure, timers and serial port of the 8051

Model answer

Interrupt structure

The 8051 has five interrupt sources, all vectored:

SourceFlagType
External interrupt 0INT0External
Timer 0 overflowTF0Internal
External interrupt 1INT1External
Timer 1 overflowTF1Internal
Serial portRI / TIInternal

Working: the microcontroller can be configured so that on the occurrence of an interrupt it temporarily terminates or pauses the main program, executes the interrupt subroutine, and when that completes the main program resumes as usual. Interrupts are enabled through the IE (Interrupt Enable) register — writing MOV IE, #82H sets bit 7 (EA, enable all) and bit 1 (ET0, enable Timer 0).

Timers and counters

The 8051 has two 16-bit timer/counters, Timer 0 and Timer 1. They can be used either as timers to generate a time delay or as counters to count events happening outside the microcontroller — the same timer-versus-counter distinction as elsewhere in the course: a timer counts a periodic clock, a counter counts aperiodic external events.

Because the 8051 has an 8-bit architecture, each 16-bit timer is accessed as two separate registers, a low byte and a high byte — TL0/TH0 and TL1/TH1. The mode is set through the TMOD register, written exactly like memory because the 8051 is memory-mapped: MOV TMOD, #01H.

Serial port

The 8051 contains one serial port or UART. It is full duplex, so it can transmit and receive simultaneously. Two port pins provide the interface: P3.0 is the receive pin (RXD) and P3.1 is the transmit pin (TXD). The port can be programmed to operate in one of four different modes and at a range of frequencies, the baud rate being generated from Timer 1.

Q8.3   Type S  ·  10 marks

Select an 8051 family member for three applications

Using the Atmel series table, select a part for: (i) a battery-powered remote control with 12 buttons, (ii) a washing machine controller needing three timers, (iii) a data logger requiring 200 bytes of working RAM. Justify each.

Model answer
ApplicationPartJustification
(i) Battery remote controlAT89C1051Only 15 I/O pins are needed for a 12-button matrix plus an IR output — well inside its 15. Runs at 3 V, which is decisive for battery life, and comes in a 20-pin package, minimising size and cost. 1K ROM and 64 bytes RAM are ample for scanning a keypad and emitting IR codes
(ii) Washing machine controllerAT89C52Three timers are required and only the C52, C2051, LV52 offer three. The C52 gives 8K ROM for the wash-programme tables, 256 bytes RAM, 32 I/O pins for sensors, valves, motor and display, and eight interrupt sources. 5 V mains-derived supply is available, so the low-voltage parts offer no advantage
(iii) Data logger with 200 bytes RAMAT89C52Only the AT89C52 provides 256 bytes of RAM; every other part in the table has 128 bytes or fewer, which cannot hold a 200-byte buffer plus the stack. This is the single deciding specification
The selection method

Work down the table filtering on the binding constraint first, then optimise the rest:

  1. I/O pins — can it physically connect to everything?
  2. RAM — will the working data fit? This is the constraint that most often eliminates parts, because 128 bytes is very little.
  3. Timers and interrupts — are there enough peripherals?
  4. ROM — will the program fit?
  5. Vcc and package — 3 V for battery products, 5 V where mains is available; 20-pin where size matters.

Case (iii) shows why RAM is checked early: no amount of ROM compensates for insufficient RAM.

Q8.5   Type S  ·  10 marks

Is the 8051 sufficient?

For each system, state whether an 8051 is sufficient and justify: (i) a traffic light controller, (ii) a digital audio effects unit, (iii) the ACVM from Unit 5, (iv) a quadcopter flight controller.

Model answer
SystemSufficient?Reasoning
Traffic light controllerYesPure sequencing with timed phases. Two 16-bit timers cover the phase timing; 32 I/O pins drive the lamp relays and read pedestrian buttons; 4 KB ROM is ample for a state machine. Cost matters at municipal volumes, and the 8051 is very low cost
Digital audio effects unitNoRequires continuous multiply-accumulate on streaming samples. At 12 clocks per instruction cycle and 8-bit arithmetic the 8051 cannot approach the required MAC rate, and 128 bytes of RAM cannot hold a delay line. This is a DSP application
ACVMYes — the deck chooses 8051 MX with 8 MB ROMCoin counting, price comparison, delivery actuation and display sequencing. The on-chip timer supplies the required 1 s resolution. Note the 8 MB external ROM is for graphics and advertisements, not for logic
Quadcopter flight controllerNoNeeds sensor fusion at several hundred hertz, floating-point PID, six or more PWM channels and multiple serial interfaces. Requires a 32-bit Cortex-M4 with an FPU — see Unit 11
The three-question test for 8051 sufficiency
  1. Is the work sequencing and comparison, or is it computation? Sequencing → 8051 is fine. Filtering, transforms or fusion → it is not.
  2. Will the working data fit in 128 bytes of RAM? This eliminates buffering applications immediately.
  3. Are the deadlines achievable at 12 clocks per instruction? A 12 MHz 8051 executes one million instructions per second — enough for a control loop at tens of hertz, not thousands.

The ACVM is instructive because it needs 8 MB of memory yet an 8-bit CPU is still correct — memory size and processing power are independent requirements, and confusing them is a common error.

Q8.6   Type S  ·  5 marks

Why does the 8051 access its 16-bit timers as two 8-bit registers?

Explain the reason and one programming hazard it creates.

Model answer

The reason. The 8051 has an 8-bit architecture — an 8-bit CPU, 8-bit accumulator and 8-bit data bus. It can therefore move only one byte at a time. A 16-bit timer value cannot cross an 8-bit bus in a single operation, so each timer is exposed as two separately addressable registers: a low byte (TL) and a high byte (TH).

The programming hazard: a torn read or write. Reading a running timer takes two instructions. If the low byte rolls over from FFH to 00H between the two reads, the two halves belong to different instants and the combined value is badly wrong.

The standard remedies: read the high byte first, then the low byte, then the high byte again, and repeat if the high byte changed; or stop the timer before reading; or read it inside an interrupt-disabled section.

The same hazard exists on any 8-bit machine handling multi-byte values — it is why 32-bit millis() values on the AVR must be copied with interrupts disabled, and why writing a 16-bit timer register requires a specific byte order.

UNIT 09

The ARM7 Processor

Module 1 · slides 99–117  ·  Types: T, C, S  ·  Weight: highest  ·  Contains CAT-1 Q1

About ARM (slide 100)

  • ARM was founded as Advanced RISC Machines in 1990.
  • ARM is the world's leading provider of RISC-based microprocessors.
  • ARM does not manufacture silicon by itself; instead it licenses ARM core designs to many semiconductor partners around the world.
  • ARM also develops technologies to assist designing with the ARM architecture, including software tools, boards, debug hardware, application software, bus architectures and peripherals.
  • Used especially in portable devices due to low power consumption and reasonable performance (MIPS/watt).

ARM processor features (slide 102) — learn this list

Slide 102 verbatim — the "key features" the CAT question asks for
  • 32/64-bit RISC processor core
  • Load and Store type architecture
  • Fast interrupt response
  • Uniform and fixed length instruction set — 32-bit ARM and 16-bit Thumb
  • Small core size and power efficiency
  • Multiple stage pipelined operation
  • Wide range of clock frequency, from 1 MHz to a few GHz
  • High performance and high code density
  • 8 / 16 / 32 / 64-bit data types
  • Various modes of operation — USR, SYS, FIQ, IRQ, SVC, ABT, UND
  • Good speed / power consumption ratio

The deck's headline: HIGH PERFORMANCE, LOWER COST, LESS POWER.

The ARM core dataflow model (slides 109–112)

These four slides explain every block in the slide-108 diagram. Each bullet below is a block you must name when explaining the diagram.

BlockFunction (deck wording)
Instruction decoderTranslates instructions before they are executed. The ARM processor, like all RISC processors, uses a load-store architecture: load instructions copy data from memory to registers in the core, and store instructions do the converse
Register fileA storage bank made up of 32-bit registers. Most instructions treat the registers as holding signed or unsigned 32-bit values
Source registersARM instructions have two source registers, Rn and Rm, and a single result or destination register, Rd. Source operands are read from the register file using the internal buses A and B respectively
Sign extend hardwareConverts signed 8-bit and 16-bit numbers to 32-bit values
ALU and MACTakes the register values Rn and Rm from the A and B buses and computes a result. Data processing instructions write the result in Rd directly to the register file. Load and store instructions use the ALU to generate an address to be held in the address register and broadcast on the address bus
Address register and incrementerFor load and store instructions the incrementer updates the address register before the core reads or writes the next register value from or to the next sequential memory location. The processor continues executing instructions until an exception or interrupt changes the normal execution flow
Barrel shifterRegister Rm can alternatively be preprocessed in the barrel shifter before it enters the ALU. After passing through the functional units, the result in Rd is written back to the register file using the Result bus

The barrel shifter's five shift types (slide 112)

AbbreviationNameWhat it does
LSLLogical Shift LeftShifts left, zeros in at the right — multiplies by 2n
LSRLogical Shift RightShifts right, zeros in at the left — unsigned divide by 2n
ASRArithmetic Shift RightShifts right, copies the sign bit in — signed divide by 2n
RORRotate RightBits shifted out at the right re-enter at the left
RRXRotate Right ExtendedA 33-bit rotate right by one, through the carry flag
Why the barrel shifter is architecturally significant

It sits in the datapath before the ALU, so a shift costs no extra instruction and no extra cycle. A single ARM instruction can shift and operate at once — for example add a register to another register shifted left by two. This is a major reason ARM achieves "high code density" despite being RISC.

Processor modes (slide 113)

The processor mode determines which registers are active and the access rights to the CPSR register itself. Each mode is either privileged or non-privileged:

PrivilegedNon-privileged
CPSR accessFull read-write access to the CPSRRead access only to the control field, but still read-write access to the condition flags
CountSixOne
ModesAbort (ABT), Fast Interrupt Request (FIQ), Interrupt Request (IRQ), Supervisor (SVC), System (SYS), Undefined (UND)User (USR)

Seven processor modes in total.

The register set — supplementary detail for a fuller answer

RegisterRole
r0 – r12General purpose
r13Stack Pointer (SP) — banked per mode
r14Link Register (LR) — holds the return address
r15Program Counter (PC)
CPSRCurrent Program Status Register — condition flags N Z C V, interrupt disable bits I and F, the Thumb bit T, and the mode bits M[4:0]
SPSRSaved Program Status Register — one per privileged mode except System

ARM7 has 37 registers in total: 31 general-purpose and 6 status registers. Only 16 plus the CPSR are visible at any one time; the rest are banked and swap in when the mode changes.

Why banking gives "fast interrupt response"

FIQ mode banks r8–r14, so a fast interrupt handler has seven private registers available immediately and does not need to save them to the stack. That removes the usual push/pop overhead at the start and end of a handler, which is precisely what the feature list means by fast interrupt response.

Theory, comparison and situation questions

PYQ   CAT-1 Q1  ·  Type T  ·  10 marks

Describe the ARM architecture with a neat block diagram and explain its key features

Model answer — full exam format

Suggested mark split: introduction 1 · block diagram 3 · block explanation 3 · features 2 · modes and applications 1.

Introduction

ARM, founded as Advanced RISC Machines in 1990, is the world's leading provider of RISC-based microprocessors. ARM does not manufacture silicon itself; it licenses its core designs to semiconductor partners worldwide, and also supplies the surrounding technology — software tools, development boards, debug hardware, application software, bus architectures and peripherals. ARM cores are used especially in portable devices because of their low power consumption at reasonable performance, measured as MIPS per watt.

Block diagram

Explanation of the blocks

  • Instruction decode and control — translates instructions before they are executed and generates the control signals for every other block.
  • Register bank (register file) — a storage bank of 32-bit registers, r0 to r15. Most instructions treat them as holding signed or unsigned 32-bit values. r13 is the stack pointer, r14 the link register and r15 the program counter.
  • Source registers — ARM instructions have two source registers, Rn and Rm, and a single destination register Rd. The operands are read out of the register file onto the internal A bus and B bus respectively.
  • Barrel shifter — Rm may optionally be preprocessed here before entering the ALU. It provides five shift types: LSL, LSR, ASR, ROR and RRX. This allows a shift and an operation in a single instruction.
  • ALU and MAC — takes the values on the A and B buses and computes a result. Data-processing instructions write the result to Rd directly; load and store instructions instead use the ALU to generate an address, held in the address register and driven onto the address bus.
  • Multiply register — holds the operand and partial products for the multiply and multiply-accumulate unit.
  • Address register and incrementer — the address register drives A[31:0]. For load and store instructions the incrementer updates it before the core reads or writes the next register value from the next sequential memory location, which is what makes block transfers efficient.
  • Sign-extend hardware — converts signed 8-bit and 16-bit values loaded from memory into 32-bit values.
  • Data in / data out registers — buffer data arriving from and leaving to the D[31:0] data bus.
  • Result bus — carries the value in Rd back to the register file after it has passed through the functional units.

Key features

(Give the eleven-point slide-102 list.)

Processor modes

The processor mode determines which registers are active and the access rights to the CPSR. There are seven modes: six privileged — abort, fast interrupt request, interrupt request, supervisor, system and undefined — and one non-privileged, user. A privileged mode allows full read-write access to the CPSR; a non-privileged mode allows only read access to the control field, but still permits read-write access to the condition flags.

Applications

Home appliances, consumer electronics, home automation and security, computer components, automotive, health care, military, industrial, business, retail, communications, avionics and banking.

Two deck inconsistencies to handle carefully

The comparison table on slide 123 lists ARM as using a modified Harvard architecture. That is true of ARM9 and the Cortex cores, but the ARM7 core shown in the slide-108 block diagram is Von Neumann — a single data bus D[31:0] carries both instructions and data. If a question asks about ARM in general, quote the deck; if it asks about ARM7 specifically, say Von Neumann and note the change from ARM9 onward.

Slide 59 also pairs microprocessors with "Von Neumann and RISC" — for ARM7 that pairing happens to be exactly right.

Q9.1   Type T  ·  10 marks

Explain the ARM core dataflow model

Model answer

(Draw the slide-108 diagram and trace one instruction through it — that trace is what distinguishes this question from Q1.)

Tracing a data-processing instruction: ADD Rd, Rn, Rm, LSL #2

  1. The address register drives the PC onto A[31:0]; the instruction arrives on D[31:0] into the data in register.
  2. The instruction decoder translates it and raises the control signals for the remaining blocks.
  3. Rn is read from the register bank onto the A bus; Rm is read onto the B bus.
  4. Rm passes through the barrel shifter, which applies LSL #2 — at no extra cycle cost, because the shifter is in the datapath.
  5. The ALU adds the A-bus value to the shifted B-bus value.
  6. The result is written back to Rd in the register file over the Result bus.
  7. Meanwhile the incrementer has advanced the address register so the next instruction can be fetched.

Tracing a load instruction: LDR Rd, [Rn, #offset]

  1. Rn is read onto the A bus and the offset supplied to the B bus.
  2. The ALU is used to generate an address rather than a data result — this is the key difference the deck emphasises.
  3. The address is held in the address register and broadcast on A[31:0].
  4. Data returns on D[31:0] into the data in register.
  5. If the value is a signed byte or halfword, the sign extend hardware converts it to 32 bits.
  6. The value is written into Rd in the register file.

The load-store principle

The ARM processor, like all RISC processors, uses a load-store architecture: only load and store instructions access memory, and all arithmetic and logic operates register to register. The processor continues executing until an exception or interrupt changes the normal execution flow.

The consequence worth stating: a variable in memory must be loaded, operated on, and stored back — three instructions where a CISC machine might use one — which is why RISC needs many registers and why ARM provides sixteen.

Q9.2   Type T  ·  10 marks

Explain the ARM processor modes and register set

Model answer

Processor modes

The processor mode determines which registers are active and the access rights to the CPSR register itself. Each mode is either privileged or non-privileged.

ModeAbbrev.PrivilegeEntered when
UserUSRNon-privilegedNormal application execution
SystemSYSPrivilegedPrivileged tasks using the user register set
SupervisorSVCPrivilegedReset, or a software interrupt
AbortABTPrivilegedA memory access fails
UndefinedUNDPrivilegedAn undefined instruction is executed
Interrupt RequestIRQPrivilegedA normal interrupt occurs
Fast Interrupt RequestFIQPrivilegedA high-priority interrupt occurs

Access rights: a privileged mode allows full read-write access to the CPSR. A non-privileged mode allows only read access to the control field of the CPSR, but still allows read-write access to the condition flags.

Register set

ARM7 has 37 registers — 31 general purpose and 6 status. At any instant 16 general registers (r0–r15) plus the CPSR are visible; the remainder are banked and are substituted automatically when the mode changes.

  • r0–r12 general purpose · r13 = SP · r14 = LR (link register, holds the return address) · r15 = PC
  • CPSR — condition flags N, Z, C, V; interrupt disable bits I and F; the T bit selecting ARM or Thumb state; and the mode bits M[4:0]
  • SPSR — a Saved Program Status Register exists in each privileged mode except System, holding the CPSR of the interrupted program so it can be restored

Why banking matters

Each privileged mode banks its own r13 and r14, giving every exception handler a private stack pointer and return address. FIQ additionally banks r8–r12, so a fast interrupt handler has private working registers available immediately and need not save them. That is the mechanism behind the "fast interrupt response" listed among ARM's features.

Q9.3   Type C  ·  10 marks

Compare the ARM7 with the 8051

Model answer
Parameter8051ARM7
IntroducedIntel, 1980Advanced RISC Machines, 1990
Bus width8-bit32-bit
Instruction setCISC, variable lengthRISC, uniform fixed length (32-bit ARM, 16-bit Thumb)
Memory accessInstructions may operate on memory directlyLoad-store — only load and store touch memory
Speed12 clocks per instruction cycle1 clock per instruction
PipelineNoneMultiple stage pipelined — three stages in ARM7
Registers32 general purpose, 8-bit37 registers, 32-bit, with mode banking
Clock rangeTypically 12–24 MHz1 MHz to a few GHz
ModesNoneSeven — USR, SYS, FIQ, IRQ, SVC, ABT, UND
InterruptsFive sourcesVectored exceptions with banked FIQ registers for fast response
Barrel shifterNoYes — five shift types in the datapath
Business modelManufactured by Intel and licenseesARM licenses the core; it does not fabricate silicon
CostVery lowLow for its performance
Suited toSimple, low-cost dedicated controlPortable devices needing performance per watt

The one-line summary

The 8051 is chosen when the job is simple and cost dominates; the ARM7 is chosen when performance per watt dominates. A vending machine controller and a smartphone are both embedded systems, but only one of them needs a 32-bit pipelined RISC core.

The quantitative point to include: at the same clock frequency the ARM7 executes roughly twelve times as many instructions as the 8051, because of the 1-clock versus 12-clock instruction cycle. That single ratio explains most of the other differences.

Q9.4   Type S  ·  10 marks

Why is ARM dominant in portable devices?

Explain, referring to specific architectural features, why ARM cores are used in almost all mobile phones, tablets and wearables rather than x86 processors.

Model answer
Requirement of a portable deviceARM feature that satisfies it
Battery lifeLow power consumption at reasonable performance — good MIPS/watt. The deck names this as the specific reason ARM is used in portable devices
Small physical sizeSmall core size, leaving die area for GPU, modem and memory on the same SoC
Limited memoryHigh code density, especially in 16-bit Thumb state, so firmware occupies less Flash
Responsive user interfaceFast interrupt response via banked FIQ registers
Performance when neededMulti-stage pipelined operation at roughly one instruction per clock, over a clock range from 1 MHz to a few GHz
Low unit cost at huge volumeThe licensing model — see below
Multitasking OS supportSeven processor modes with privileged and non-privileged separation, which an OS needs to protect itself from applications

The business reason, which matters as much as the technical one

ARM does not manufacture silicon by itself; it licenses its core designs to many semiconductor partners. This has three consequences that no vertically integrated manufacturer can match:

  1. Competition among licensees drives per-unit prices down.
  2. Each licensee integrates the core with its own peripherals — a modem vendor, a camera vendor and an automotive vendor all build different SoCs around the same proven core.
  3. One software ecosystem serves all of them, because the instruction set is common. ARM also supplies the software tools, boards, debug hardware, application software, bus architectures and peripherals that make adoption cheap.

Why not x86

x86 is a CISC architecture designed when performance, not energy, was the deciding factor. It carries decades of backward-compatible instruction decoding, which costs die area and power on every instruction fetched. For a device whose deciding metric is power, that overhead is paid continuously and cannot be switched off.

Tie back to Module 1's framework: a smartphone's dominant design metrics are power and size, with unit cost close behind. ARM optimises exactly those three, which is why it wins the class of products defined by them.

Q9.5   Type S  ·  10 marks

Explain the ARM partnership model and its consequences for an embedded designer

Model answer

The model

ARM does not manufacture silicon by itself. It designs processor cores and licenses those designs to semiconductor partners around the world, who integrate them into their own chips and fabricate them. ARM additionally develops technologies to assist designing with its architecture — software tools, development boards, debug hardware, application software, bus architectures and peripherals.

Consequences for the designer

ConsequenceWhy it matters in practice
One instruction set, many suppliersFirmware and toolchain skills transfer between vendors. Second-sourcing is possible, which matters for a product with a 15-year life
Enormous peripheral varietyThe core is common but the peripherals differ, so processor selection becomes largely peripheral set analysis — exactly the Module 3 criterion
Low cost through competitionMany licensees compete on price for the same core
Mature ecosystemARM supplies the tools, boards and debug hardware, so "is the processor supported by appropriate and adequate tools?" — one of Module 3's four opening questions — is almost always answered yes
Scalable familyCortex-M0+ through Cortex-A: a design can move up or down the family with the same skills as requirements change

The selection question therefore shifts from "which architecture?" to "which vendor's implementation of this architecture has the peripherals I need at the power I can afford?" — which is precisely why the Module 3 case studies name specific parts such as the Cortex-M3 and Cortex-A53 rather than simply saying "ARM".

Q9.6   Type T  ·  5 marks

Explain the barrel shifter and its five shift operations, and why it improves code density

Model answer

What it is. The barrel shifter is a combinational unit placed in the datapath between the register bank and the ALU. Register Rm can alternatively be preprocessed in the barrel shifter before it enters the ALU.

(Give the five-shift table: LSL, LSR, ASR, ROR, RRX.)

Why it improves code density and speed

Because the shifter is in the datapath rather than a separate instruction, a shift is performed in the same cycle as the operation that uses it. A single ARM instruction can therefore do what a conventional processor needs two or three instructions for:

Common uses: address calculation for array indexing (base + index << 2 for a 32-bit array), fast multiplication by constants, and constructing bit masks.

This is a direct contributor to the deck's feature "high performance and high code density" — RISC machines normally suffer poor code density because their instructions are simple, and the barrel shifter is one of the mechanisms ARM uses to recover it.

UNIT 10

The PIC Microcontroller and Family Comparison

Module 1 · slides 118–124  ·  Types: T, C, S  ·  Weight: medium  ·  Closes Module 1

PIC16F877A features (slide 118)

  • Powerful (200 nanosecond instruction execution) yet easy to program (RISC instructions).
  • CMOS FLASH-based 8-bit microcontroller, packing Microchip's PIC architecture into a 40-pin dual in-line (DIP) package.
  • 256 bytes of EEPROM data memory · self programming · an ICD (in-circuit debugger) · 2 comparators.
  • 8 channels of 10-bit analog-to-digital conversion.
  • 2 input capture / output compare / PWM functions.
  • A synchronous serial port configurable as either 3-wire SPI or 2-wire I²C.
  • A USART.

Memory (slide 119)

MemorySizePurpose
Flash program ROM8 K, 14 bits wideProgram storage. Each of the 35 RISC instructions fits in just one 14-bit wide location, permitting fast 200 ns execution at the maximum 20 MHz clock
Data RAM368 bytes, 8 bits wideVolatile "File Register" locations for temporary storage of data
EEPROM256 bytesNon-volatile storage of calibration data and user-customised option settings
Why a 14-bit program word matters — a Harvard consequence

The program memory is 14 bits wide while data memory is 8 bits wide. That is only possible in a Harvard architecture, where the two memories are physically separate and need not share a word width.

Because every one of the 35 instructions fits in exactly one 14-bit location, instruction fetch is a single access and execution is uniform — which is what delivers the 200 ns instruction time and makes the pipeline simple. A Von Neumann machine with an 8-bit bus would need two fetches per instruction.

Theory, comparison and situation questions

Q10.1   Type T  ·  10 marks

Describe the PIC16F877A with a neat block diagram and explain its features

Model answer

Introduction

The PIC16F877A is a CMOS FLASH-based 8-bit microcontroller from Microchip, supplied in a 40-pin DIP package. It is powerful — 200 nanosecond instruction execution — yet easy to program because it uses a RISC instruction set of only 35 instructions. It uses a Harvard architecture with separate program and data memories.

Block diagram

(Draw the slide-120 hardware block diagram: the 14-bit Flash program memory and program counter feeding an instruction register and decoder; the 8-bit ALU with working register W; the 368-byte file register RAM; the 256-byte EEPROM; five I/O ports A–E; three timers; the 10-bit 8-channel ADC; the synchronous serial port; the USART; the two comparators; and the oscillator and reset circuitry.)

Memory organisation

(Give the three-row memory table. Emphasise the 14-bit program word and the one-instruction-per-location property.)

Peripherals

(Give the seven-row special-functions table.)

Key features summarised

  • 8-bit CMOS Flash microcontroller with self programming and an in-circuit debugger
  • 35 RISC instructions, each a single 14-bit word, executing in 200 ns at 20 MHz
  • 8 K Flash program memory, 368 bytes RAM, 256 bytes EEPROM
  • Three timers, 10-bit 8-channel ADC, two CCP/PWM modules, two comparators
  • SPI, I²C and USART serial interfaces
  • 8-bit parallel slave port allowing the PIC to appear as a peripheral on a host bus

Applications

Industrial control, instrumentation, automotive subsystems, motor control using the CCP/PWM modules, and any application needing on-chip analog conversion with serial connectivity.
