Slide 123 lists the 8051 as Von Neumann, but slide 79 defines it as a Harvard architecture device. Slide 79 is correct; note the discrepancy if you reproduce this table.

The row that explains the rest. The 8051 needs 12 clocks per instruction, the PIC 4, and the AVR and ARM just 1. At equal clock frequency the AVR does twelve times the work of the 8051. That single ratio drives the "known for" row: the 8051 survives on cost and ubiquity, the PIC and AVR on cheap effectiveness, and ARM on high speed operation.

Selection summary: 8051 for the cheapest possible dedicated control · PIC where rich analog peripherals and industrial support matter · AVR for easy development and the Arduino ecosystem · ARM where 32-bit performance, an OS or heavy connectivity is required.

Q10.3   Type S  ·  10 marks

PIC or 8051?

For each system choose between a PIC16F877A and an 8051 and justify: (i) a battery-monitoring system reading six cell voltages, (ii) a simple lift indicator panel, (iii) a motor speed controller needing PWM, (iv) a data logger storing calibration constants.

Model answer
SystemChoiceDeciding factor
(i) Six-cell battery monitorPIC16F877ANeeds six analog channels. The PIC has an 8-channel 10-bit ADC on chip; the 8051 has no ADC at all and would need six external converters or a multiplexer plus an ADC, adding cost, board area and pins
(ii) Lift indicator panel8051Purely digital: read floor switches, drive seven-segment displays. No analog, no PWM, no serial. The 8051 is very low cost and entirely sufficient — choosing the PIC would pay for peripherals that are never used
(iii) Motor speed controllerPIC16F877ANeeds hardware PWM. The PIC provides two CCP modules with input capture, output compare and PWM. The 8051 has no PWM hardware, so PWM must be bit-banged in software, consuming CPU time and giving jittery output
(iv) Data logger with calibration constantsPIC16F877ANeeds non-volatile storage. The PIC has 256 bytes of on-chip EEPROM explicitly for "calibration data and user-customised option settings"; the 8051 has none and would need an external EEPROM over SPI or I²C
The method: peripheral set analysis

Three of the four cases are decided not by CPU power but by which peripherals are on the chip. This is precisely Module 3's third selection step — peripheral set analysis, covering on-chip RAM, ROM, I/O ports and ADC.

The cost argument in case (ii) is equally important: choosing the more capable part when it is not needed increases unit cost in a high-volume product for no benefit. Matching capability to requirement in both directions is what the question tests.

Q10.4   Type S  ·  10 marks

Map a design's requirements onto PIC16F877A peripherals

A greenhouse controller must read three analog sensors, drive two fans by PWM, communicate with a PC over serial and with an external EEPROM, log data, and detect when a voltage crosses a reference. Show that a single PIC16F877A can serve, mapping each requirement to a specific peripheral.

Model answer
RequirementPIC16F877A peripheralPins / notes
Three analog sensors10-bit, 8-channel ADCAnalog inputs on Ports A and E — three of eight channels used, five spare
Two fans by PWMTwo CCP modules in PWM modeRC2/CCP1 and RC1/CCP2 — exactly two, so both are consumed
Serial link to a PCUSARTRC6/TX and RC7/RX
External EEPROMSynchronous serial port as SPI or I²CSDI, SDO, SCK
Local non-volatile storage256 bytes on-chip EEPROMCalibration constants and thresholds — may remove the need for the external EEPROM entirely
Periodic sampling scheduleTimer 2 with the PR2 period registerNo external pins needed — ideal for a purely internal periodic interrupt
Voltage crossing a referenceTwo analog comparators with programmable referencePort A — detects the crossing in hardware, with no CPU polling
Program storage8 K Flash, 14-bit wordsAmple for a controller of this size
Working data368 bytes RAMSufficient for sensor buffers and averaging

Conclusion

A single PIC16F877A satisfies every requirement with peripherals to spare. The binding constraint is the CCP modules: there are exactly two, and the design needs exactly two. Adding a third PWM output would force either software PWM, an external PWM chip, or a different part — so that is the specification to flag as having no margin.

The two design insights to state

1. Timer 2 is the right choice for the sampling schedule precisely because it has no external pins — it cannot conflict with any I/O requirement, and the PR2 register makes the period directly programmable.

2. The comparators remove CPU work. Detecting a threshold crossing in hardware raises an interrupt only when it happens, rather than requiring the CPU to sample and compare continuously — the same event-triggered versus time-triggered argument from Unit 2.

Q10.5   Type S  ·  5 marks

A product must migrate from a PIC16F877A to an ARM Cortex-M. What triggers such a migration, and what must be re-engineered?

Model answer

What triggers the migration

TriggerPIC16F877A limit
Program grows beyond capacity8 K Flash
Buffers or a protocol stack exceed RAM368 bytes
Floating-point or filtering added8-bit ALU, no FPU
Loop rate raised200 ns per instruction, 4 clocks per instruction
More than two PWM channelsTwo CCP modules
Networking added — Ethernet, USB, CANNot available on this part
An operating system is requiredNo MMU, insufficient RAM

What must be re-engineered

  • All peripheral initialisation code. Register names, bit positions and clock trees are entirely different — this is usually the largest part of the effort.
  • The toolchain. A new compiler, debugger and programmer; Module 3 lists "is the processor supported by appropriate and adequate tools?" as a gating question for exactly this reason.
  • Any assembly language — the 35-instruction PIC set and the ARM instruction set share nothing.
  • Interrupt structure — a flat PIC interrupt model becomes ARM's vectored, priority-based scheme.
  • Hardware — different package, 3.3 V rather than 5 V logic, and therefore level shifting for any 5 V peripherals.

What transfers: the application logic, if it was written in portable C with hardware access isolated behind a driver layer. This is the practical argument for a hardware abstraction layer: it turns a rewrite into a port.

Q10.6   Type C  ·  5 marks

Why does the PIC use a 14-bit program word with 8-bit data, and what does that buy?

Model answer

It is possible only because the PIC is Harvard. Program and data memories are physically separate with independent buses, so they are not obliged to share a word width. A Von Neumann machine, having one memory and one bus, must use one width for both.

What the 14-bit width buys. Each of the 35 RISC instructions fits in exactly one 14-bit location. That has three consequences:

  1. One fetch per instruction. An 8-bit-wide program memory would need two or three fetches to assemble a single instruction, tripling the memory traffic.
  2. Uniform timing. Every instruction occupies one word and, apart from branches, one cycle — which is what delivers the quoted 200 ns instruction execution at 20 MHz and makes worst-case timing analysis easy in a real-time system.
  3. Simple pipelining. Fixed-length instructions make fetch and execute stages uniform, so the next instruction is fetched while the current one executes.

The cost. Program memory cannot be reallocated as data memory, and the 14-bit width is unusual, so the program memory is not byte-addressable in the way a Von Neumann machine's is.

This is a concrete instance of the general Harvard trade-off: speed and uniformity bought at the cost of flexibility in memory allocation.

UNIT 11

Processor Selection Criteria

Module 3 · slides 3–7  ·  Types: T, S  ·  Weight: highest  ·  Contains CAT-1 Q5  ·  One framework, applied everywhere

Module 3 in one sentence

Forty-nine slides carrying one idea applied three times. Learn the framework below and every Module 3 question becomes the same question with a different product.

The four opening questions (slides 4–5)

Is it available in a suitable implementation?"What good is choosing the highest performing processor if the cost of goods makes your product noncompetitive in the marketplace?"

Is the processor capable of sufficient performance?"The processor must be able to do the job on time."

Is the processor supported by an appropriate operating system?"Porting the RTOS kernel to a new or different microprocessor architecture and having it specifically optimised to take advantage of the low-level performance features of that microprocessor is not a task for the faint-hearted."

Is the processor supported by appropriate and adequate tools?"Good tools are critical to project success. At a minimum, you'll need a good cross-compiler and good debugging support."

Note what these four are about: only one concerns raw capability. The others concern cost, ecosystem and tooling — the practical realities that sink projects.

Types of processor (slide 6)

To design an efficient embedded system, selection of the right processor is a very important and challenging task. Three types:

TypeDeck descriptionChoose when
µPOffered in 4 to 64-bit sizes with distinct features — cost, speed, number of CPU cores, address and data lines. Used in everything from simple toys to network routersComputing power, large memory or an OS is required
µCPlays an important role in embedded system design and is majorly used in low-end to high-end control applicationsThe job is dedicated control with modest memory
DSPMajorly used for high computation intensive applications such as image processing, communication devices, voice-to-text converterThe inner loop is multiply-accumulate over streaming data

If a question mentions images, audio or signal filtering, a DSP belongs in your answer.

The five-step selection sequence (slide 7) — the spine of every Module 3 answer

Application requirement analysisUnderstand the purpose of the application and arrive at specific requirements.

Processor architecture analysisMCS-51, ARM, PIC, PowerPC, MIPS and so on.

Peripheral set analysisIncludes on-chip RAM, ROM, I/O ports and ADC, and specialised processing units — FPU, MMU, DMA.

Technical analysisExecution speed, operating voltage, power consumption, and data and address bus size.

Non-technical analysisCost, software tools, package type, vendor reputation, support.

Memorise the five names in order

Application → Architecture → Peripheral set → Technical → Non-technical. Writing these five as headings and filling each for the product in the question produces a complete, well-structured answer to any "select a processor" question, even one you have never seen.

The ten criteria that fill the justification table

Taken from the official answer key's drone table. These generalise to any system — change only the justification column.

Selection criterionWhat you argue
Processing speedThe real-time loop rate the application demands
Floating-point capabilityPID control, filtering, navigation mathematics
Timers / PWMNumber of actuators to drive
Communication interfacesSPI/I²C for sensors, UART for GPS and telemetry
Interrupt performanceDeterministic sensor acquisition
Flash memorySize of the control and navigation firmware
SRAMRun-time buffers and control-loop state
External storageLogging, images, long-term field data
Power consumptionBattery life or flight duration
ReliabilityWatchdog and fault-detection support

Theory and situation questions

PYQ   CAT-1 Q5  ·  Type S  ·  10 marks

Choose the microcontroller and memory for an agricultural drone

Choose the appropriate microcontroller and memory for designing an agricultural drone. Draw a neat block diagram and explain the working of the drone. Justify the processor and memory selection criteria.

Model answer — full exam format

Suggested mark split: block diagram 3 · working 2 · processor and memory choice 2 · criteria table 3.

Introduction

An agricultural drone is a hard real-time, safety-critical, battery-powered embedded system. It must stabilise itself continuously by fusing inertial data, navigate by GPS, drive several motors precisely, and carry an application payload such as a sprayer or a camera. Loss of the control loop means loss of the aircraft, so determinism and reliability outrank raw throughput.

Block diagram

Working

  1. The IMU supplies accelerometer and gyroscope data at a high rate over SPI or I²C; the barometer supplies altitude; the GPS/GNSS module supplies position over UART.
  2. The STM32F4 fuses these readings into an attitude and position estimate, typically with a complementary or Kalman filter running in the floating-point unit.
  3. A PID control loop compares the estimated attitude with the desired attitude and computes a correction for each motor.
  4. The corrections are emitted as PWM signals from the timer peripherals to the Electronic Speed Controllers, which drive the BLDC motors and propellers. This loop runs continuously at several hundred hertz.
  5. The telemetry link — LoRa or Wi-Fi — exchanges commands and status with the ground station.
  6. The payload — sprayer, camera or agricultural sensor — is actuated according to the mission plan and the current GPS position.
  7. Field data and images are logged to the SD card, while calibration constants live in Flash and the live control state in SRAM.

Processor selection

Chosen: STM32F4 series, ARM Cortex-M4 core.

AttributeProvision
Core32-bit ARM Cortex-M4, RISC, load-store
ClockUp to 168 MHz
Floating pointSingle-precision FPU plus DSP instructions
Timers / PWMMultiple advanced timers, enough PWM channels for four or more ESCs
InterfacesSPI, I²C, multiple UARTs, CAN, USB, SDIO
InterruptsNVIC with priority levels and low, deterministic latency
ReliabilityIndependent and window watchdog timers, brown-out detection

Memory selection

MemoryProvisionHolds
FlashUp to 1 MB internalFlight-control firmware, navigation software, mission plans
SRAMUp to 192 KB internalReal-time IMU, GPS and control-loop data; filter state
EEPROM / emulatedSmallSensor calibration constants, configuration
External SD cardGB scaleAgricultural images and long-term field data logs

Processor and memory selection criteria

Selection criterionJustification
Processing speedReal-time stabilisation requires rapid sensor processing and motor control
Floating-point capabilityUseful for PID control, filtering and navigation calculations
Timers / PWMRequired to control multiple ESCs and motors
Communication interfacesSPI/I²C for sensors, UART for GPS and telemetry
Interrupt performanceRequired for deterministic real-time sensor acquisition
Flash memoryStores the flight-control program and navigation software
SRAMStores real-time IMU, GPS and control-loop data
External storageRequired for agricultural images and long-term field data
Power consumptionLower processor power improves drone flight duration
ReliabilityThe processor must support watchdog and fault-detection mechanisms

Conclusion

An 8-bit ATmega328P would be wholly inadequate here: no floating-point unit, 16 MHz, and 2 KB of SRAM — far too little for sensor fusion state. The Cortex-M4 supplies hardware floating point, a deterministic nested vectored interrupt controller, ample PWM channels and watchdog support, at a power budget that preserves flight time. That combination of real-time determinism, floating-point mathematics and low power is the binding constraint, and it is what selects the STM32F4.

Q11.1   Type T  ·  10 marks

Explain the criteria for selecting a processor for an embedded system

Model answer

Introduction

To design an efficient embedded system, selection of the right processor is a very important and challenging task. Three types of processor are available: the microprocessor, offered in 4 to 64-bit sizes and used in everything from simple toys to network routers; the microcontroller, majorly used in low-end to high-end control applications; and the digital signal processor, majorly used for high computation intensive applications such as image processing, communication devices and voice-to-text conversion.

Four gatekeeping questions

(Give the four opening questions with their deck justifications.)

The five-step sequence of analysis

(Give the five steps with their contents.)

Applying the framework — the ten criteria

(Give the ten-row criteria table.)

Conclusion

Selection is not a search for the fastest processor. The binding constraint of the application selects the processor. A battery-powered wearable is selected by power; a flight controller by determinism and floating point; a camera by multiply-accumulate throughput; an ATM by security. Identify the binding constraint first, and the rest of the answer follows.

Q11.2   Type S  ·  10 marks

Choose a processor and memory for a wearable fitness tracker

Draw a block diagram, explain the working, and justify the selection criteria.

Model answer

Binding constraint: battery life. The device must run for days from a tiny cell, so ultra-low power dominates every other consideration. State this in the opening paragraph — it justifies everything that follows.

Working

  1. The accelerometer samples motion continuously and raises an interrupt when a step-like pattern occurs, so the processor can sleep between events.
  2. The optical heart-rate sensor is sampled periodically rather than continuously, to save power.
  3. The processor runs a step-detection algorithm and a heart-rate estimate, and accumulates daily totals.
  4. Results are shown on the OLED and stored in external Flash so data survives battery depletion.
  5. The BLE radio periodically wakes, syncs accumulated data to the phone, and sleeps again.

Selection

Processor: an ARM Cortex-M0+ class SoC with an integrated BLE radio, such as the nRF52 family. Memory: a few hundred KB of Flash for firmware and the BLE stack, 32–64 KB SRAM for buffers, and a small external serial Flash for activity history.

CriterionJustification
Power consumptionDominant criterion — must support deep sleep at microamp currents with wake on interrupt
Processing speedModest. Step counting and heart-rate estimation are light; a faster core would waste power
Floating pointNot required — fixed-point arithmetic is adequate and cheaper in power
Integrated radioAn SoC with on-chip BLE avoids a separate radio chip, saving board area and power
Interrupt performanceWake-on-motion lets the core stay asleep almost all the time
Flash memoryFirmware plus the BLE protocol stack, which is itself substantial
SRAMSensor buffers and radio packet buffers
External storageSerial Flash retains activity history across battery depletion
Package sizeWafer-level or small QFN to fit a wrist-worn enclosure
CostHigh-volume consumer product; unit cost matters more than NRE
The contrast to write explicitly

The drone needed a Cortex-M4 with an FPU because its constraint was real-time computation; the tracker needs a Cortex-M0+ without one because its constraint is energy. Same framework, opposite answer — that is exactly what a K2 question is testing.

Q11.3   Type S  ·  10 marks

Choose a processor and memory for a smart traffic control system

The system serves a four-way junction, adapts signal timing to real-time vehicle density measured by cameras, and reports to a central control room.

Model answer

Binding constraint: image processing throughput. Vehicle counting from camera frames is a computer-vision workload, which pushes decisively away from a microcontroller.

Working

  1. Four cameras, one per approach, capture frames continuously.
  2. The processor runs a vehicle-detection algorithm on each frame to estimate queue length per approach.
  3. A scheduling algorithm allocates green time in proportion to measured density, subject to minimum and maximum green times for safety.
  4. Signal outputs drive the lamp relays through isolated drivers.
  5. Traffic statistics are logged locally and transmitted to the control room over Ethernet or 4G.
  6. A watchdog and a hardwired failsafe force the junction into all-flashing-amber if the processor stops responding.

Selection

Processor: an application processor — an ARM Cortex-A53 class SoC, as used in the deck's rugged handheld case study, ideally with an integrated GPU or NPU for the vision workload. Memory: 1–2 GB DRAM for frame buffers, 8–16 GB eMMC or SD for the operating system and logs, plus a small EEPROM for configuration.

CriterionJustification
Processing speedReal-time vision on four camera streams demands application-processor performance
Parallelism / acceleratorA GPU or NPU handles the convolution-heavy detection far more efficiently than a scalar CPU
Operating system supportLinux is needed for camera drivers, networking stack and file system — one of the deck's four opening questions
Memory bandwidthFrame buffers are large and must move at video rate; DRAM is mandatory
Communication interfacesMIPI or USB for cameras, Ethernet or 4G for the control room
Non-volatile storageeMMC or SD holds the OS, application and traffic logs
ReliabilityWatchdog plus an independent hardwired failsafe — a junction is safety-critical
Power consumptionMains-powered, so power is a thermal and cost issue rather than a battery-life one
Environmental ratingRoadside cabinet — wide temperature range, dust and vibration
Tools and long-term supplyA mature toolchain and a decade of part availability, since the installation must last
The three-way contrast to close with

Tracker → Cortex-M0+ (energy-bound) · Drone → Cortex-M4 (determinism-bound) · Traffic system → Cortex-A (throughput-bound). Naming that progression proves you can apply the framework rather than recall an answer.

Q11.4   Type S  ·  10 marks

µP, µC or DSP?

For each application state which of the three processor types the deck's slide 6 would indicate, and justify: (i) a voice-to-text converter, (ii) a microwave oven controller, (iii) a network router, (iv) a hearing aid, (v) an electronic toy.

Model answer
ApplicationTypeJustification
Voice-to-text converterDSPNamed explicitly by the deck as a high computation intensive application. Continuous filtering, FFT and feature extraction on an audio stream — a multiply-accumulate workload
Microwave oven controllerµCA low-end control application: keypad, display, timer, magnetron relay and door interlock. Dedicated, cost-sensitive, no computation
Network routerµPThe deck names routers explicitly among µP applications. Needs an OS, protocol stack, file system and large external memory
Hearing aidDSP, or a DSP-class ASIPReal-time audio filtering and noise suppression with deterministic low latency, under extreme power and size constraints
Electronic toyµCThe deck lists simple toys at the low end of the µP range, but a dedicated low-cost µC is the normal choice — small-scale, not time critical, and unit cost dominates
The single question that separates the three

What does the inner loop do?

  • Compare and actuate → microcontroller. Thresholds, sequencing, state machines.
  • Multiply-accumulate over a data stream → DSP. Filters, transforms, codecs.
  • Manage tasks, memory and protocols → microprocessor. Anything needing an operating system.

Real products often combine them: a smartphone contains a µP for the OS, DSPs for the modem and audio, and dedicated ASPs as GPU and NPU — the deck's own slides 73–76.

Q11.5   Type S  ·  10 marks

Apply the five-step sequence to an industrial data logger

A logger must record eight analog channels at 1 kHz for 30 days to an SD card, run from mains with battery backup, and be serviced in the field. Work the five steps of slide 7 explicitly.

Model answer

Step 1 — Application requirement analysis

Eight channels at 1 kHz = 8,000 samples per second. At 2 bytes per sample that is 16 KB/s, 57.6 MB per hour, and about 41 GB over 30 days — which immediately establishes that removable bulk storage, not on-chip memory, is required. Field servicing implies firmware update and diagnostics.

Step 2 — Processor architecture analysis

An 8-bit MCS-51 or PIC cannot sustain 8,000 conversions per second alongside file-system writes. A 32-bit ARM Cortex-M is indicated: sufficient throughput, a mature toolchain, and wide vendor choice through the ARM licensing model.

Step 3 — Peripheral set analysis

NeedPeripheral
Eight analog channelsMulti-channel ADC, ideally ≥ 12-bit, with a multiplexer
Exact 1 kHz samplingTimer-triggered conversion — software triggering would jitter
Move samples without CPU loadDMA — a specialised processing unit the deck lists explicitly
SD cardSDIO or high-speed SPI
Field diagnostics and updateUART or USB
Calibration constantsOn-chip EEPROM or an emulated Flash region

DMA is the decisive peripheral here. Without it the CPU must service 8,000 interrupts per second merely to move data; with it, the ADC fills a buffer autonomously and the CPU is interrupted only when a block is ready to write.

Step 4 — Technical analysis

Execution speed of tens of MHz is ample once DMA removes the per-sample load. Operating voltage 3.3 V. Power consumption is secondary on mains but matters during battery backup, so deep-sleep modes are wanted. A 32-bit data bus and enough address space for the file-system buffers.

Step 5 — Non-technical analysis

Cost is moderate for an industrial product. Software tools must include a maintained SD/FAT library. Package type should be solderable and available in an industrial temperature grade. Vendor reputation and support matter because the product must be manufacturable for years — a long-term-supply commitment is part of the decision.

Conclusion

An ARM Cortex-M4 class microcontroller with multi-channel ADC, DMA, SDIO and at least 128 KB SRAM for double-buffering. The binding constraint is sustained I/O throughput rather than computation, which is why DMA and buffering dominate the answer rather than clock speed.

Q11.6   Type T  ·  5 marks

Why do the deck's four opening questions emphasise cost, operating system and tools rather than performance?

Model answer

Only one of the four questions concerns capability — "is the processor capable of sufficient performance?" — and even that is phrased as "the processor must be able to do the job on time", a sufficiency test rather than a maximisation.

QuestionWhat it protects against
Suitable implementation?Choosing a technically excellent part that makes the product noncompetitive in the marketplace — the deck's own wording. A design that cannot be sold has failed regardless of its performance
Sufficient performance?Missing deadlines. Note it asks for sufficient, not maximum — over-specifying costs money and power for no benefit
Operating system support?Discovering after selection that the RTOS must be ported. The deck warns this is "not a task for the faint-hearted" — it can consume more effort than the entire application
Tools support?A part that cannot be efficiently programmed or debugged. "Good tools are critical to project success" — at minimum a good cross-compiler and good debugging support

Three of the four are about whether the project can be completed and sold, not about whether the chip is fast.

The underlying lesson: processor selection is a systems and business decision, not a benchmark comparison. This mirrors Module 1's design metrics, where time-to-market, NRE cost and flexibility sit alongside performance — and where the key challenge is optimising many metrics simultaneously rather than maximising one.
