Smart cardOptional contact and contactless (MIFARE) interface
Battery7.4 V 2600 mAh Li-ion rechargeable pack; external universal AC/DC 9.7 V 2 A adaptor
Mechanical102 × 276 × 82 mm; weight 655 g without paper roll

Why the Cortex-M3 (slides 15–17)

Slide 15, quotable

"The Cortex-M3 processor is specifically developed for high-performance, low-cost platforms for a broad range of devices including microcontrollers, automotive body systems, industrial control systems, and wireless networking and sensors."

Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (slides 18–19)

NVIC is a method of prioritising interrupts, improving the MCU's performance and reducing interrupt latency. NVIC also provides implementation schemes for handling interrupts that occur when other interrupts are being executed, or when the CPU is in the process of restoring its previous state and resuming its suspended process.

NVIC is the concrete answer to "interrupt performance" in the ten selection criteria — it is what makes a Cortex-M deterministic enough for real-time work, and it is why the drone answer names it.

Device 2 — the rugged handheld data terminal (slides 20–25)

It is built for life out in the field, integrates Corning Gorilla glass for the display, and is able to handle drops, bumps, spills, dust and vibration. With stable wireless connections and accurate, efficient data capture options, it increases productivity in logistics, express delivery, warehousing, retail and industrial manufacture.

SpecificationValue
Operating systemAndroid 10.0
Memory8 GB ROM + 1 GB RAM (16 GB + 2 GB optional)
Display4" high resolution 480 × 800 IPS TFT
Camera8 MP autofocus with LED flash
Connectivity2G, 3G, 4G, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth
SealingIP65
Scanner2D Zebra SE4710 barcode scanner
ProcessorCortex-A53

The Cortex-A53 (slide 23): "a high efficiency processor that implements the Armv8-A architecture. It has one to four cores, each with an L1 memory system and a single shared L2 cache. It can be combined with other Cortex-A CPUs in a big.LITTLE configuration."

The comparison this unit exists to teach
Spot billing machineRugged data terminal
ProcessorCortex-M3 — microcontroller classCortex-A53 — application processor class
Operating systemBare metal or a small RTOSAndroid 10.0 — a full OS
Memory1 MB Flash, 8 MB data8 GB ROM, 1 GB RAM — a thousandfold more
MMUMPU only (protection, no virtual memory)Full MMU — required by Android
CoresOneOne to four, with L1 and shared L2 cache
WhyFixed billing function, long battery life, low costCamera, barcode decoding, 4G, general applications

Both are handheld billing/data devices, yet they sit two whole processor classes apart — because one runs a fixed application and the other must run a general purpose operating system. The deciding question is the deck's third opening question: is the processor supported by an appropriate operating system?

Numericals

N12.1 — The Cortex-M3 is quoted at 1.25 DMIPS/MHz and 150 DMIPS. Verify the clock frequency.

Clock = DMIPS / (DMIPS per MHz) = 150 / 1.25 = 120 MHz This matches the quoted "120 MHz max" ✓

N12.2 — Find the energy stored in the 7.4 V 2600 mAh battery, and the runtime if the device draws an average 250 mA.

Energy = 7.4 V × 2.6 Ah = 19.24 Wh Runtime = 2600 mAh / 250 mA = 10.4 hours Enough for a full working shift, which is the design intent

N12.3 — The printer runs at 2.7 lines/sec. How long to print a 20-line bill, and how many bills per hour can be printed?

Time per bill = 20 / 2.7 = 7.4 seconds Bills per hour = 3600 / 7.4 = 486 bills/hour The printer, not the processor, limits throughput.

N12.4 — The graphical LCD is 132 × 64 pixels, monochrome. Find the frame buffer size and express it as a fraction of the 8 MB data memory.

Pixels = 132 × 64 = 8448 At 1 bit per pixel: 8448 / 8 = 1056 bytes ≈ 1 KB As a fraction of 8 MB = 1056 / 8,388,608 = 0.0126 % The display is negligible; the 8 MB exists for customer data.

Theory and situation questions

Q12.1   Type T  ·  10 marks

Explain the processor selection for a handheld spot billing machine

Model answer

Application requirement analysis

A GPRS-enabled handheld billing machine, under 500 g, serving as a handheld computer, WEB/USB enabled so the operator can produce an instant bill remotely and update transactions to the server. It must be password-protected, hold customer data in memory, and print bills on site.

Block diagram

(Draw slide 11: keypad and card reader as inputs; the Cortex-M3 at the centre; graphical LCD, impact printer and GSM/GPRS modem as outputs; 8 MB non-volatile memory, RTC and battery below.)

Processor architecture analysis

ARM 32-bit Cortex-M3 at 120 MHz, developed specifically for high-performance, low-cost platforms. Key attributes: ART Accelerator for zero-wait-state Flash execution, an MPU for memory protection, 150 DMIPS at 1.25 DMIPS/MHz, and In-System Programming allowing on-the-fly field upgrades over serial or USB.

Peripheral set analysis

RequirementPeripheral
Bill printingParallel or serial interface to the 24-column impact printer
Operator inputGPIO matrix for the 35-key keyboard
DisplayInterface to the 132 × 64 graphical LCD
Remote billingUART to the GSM/GPRS modem
Meter readingIR / IrDA port for communication with electricity meters
PC connectionRS232C and USB
PaymentSmart card interface, contact and contactless MIFARE
TimestampingBuilt-in RTC with battery backup
Interrupt handlingNVIC — prioritises interrupts, improves performance, reduces latency

Memory selection

512 K / 1024 K bytes program memory for the application, and 8 MB non-volatile data memory with 10-year retention without power, expandable to 16 MB, holding the customer database. An optional micro SD slot provides large memory backup. The 10-year retention specification is the critical one — a billing machine holds financial records that must survive a flat battery.

Technical and non-technical analysis

120 MHz is ample for menu handling, printing and modem control. The 7.4 V 2600 mAh Li-ion pack gives a full working shift. Non-technical: the Cortex-M3 has a mature toolchain through the ARM licensing ecosystem, is low cost, and is available from many vendors — satisfying the deck's opening questions on tools and suitable implementation.

Conclusion

The binding constraints are battery life, cost and field upgradeability, not computation. A Cortex-M3 meets all three; an application processor running a full OS would shorten battery life and raise cost without adding capability the task needs.

Q12.2   Type S  ·  10 marks

Cortex-M3 or Cortex-A53?

Compare the two handheld devices of this unit and explain why they use processors from different ARM families. Then decide which family suits: (i) a warehouse barcode scanner with a camera, (ii) a bus ticketing machine, (iii) a medical infusion pump.

Model answer

(Give the six-row comparison table from the key point above.)

Why they differ

The spot billing machine runs one fixed application. Its constraints are battery life, cost and weight under 500 g. A Cortex-M3 with 1 MB of Flash executes that application directly from Flash with no operating system, and sleeps between keystrokes.

The rugged terminal runs Android 10.0. That requires a full MMU for virtual memory and process isolation, gigabytes of storage, and the throughput to decode 2D barcodes and 8 MP images. Only an application processor — the Cortex-A53 implementing Armv8-A with L1 per core and a shared L2 cache — can host it.

The three cases

DeviceFamilyReason
(i) Warehouse barcode scanner with cameraCortex-A2D barcode decoding is image processing, and a camera pipeline plus wireless stack needs an OS with drivers. Same reasoning as the rugged terminal
(ii) Bus ticketing machineCortex-MFixed application — select route, compute fare, print ticket, log the transaction. Battery life and cost dominate. Directly analogous to the spot billing machine
(iii) Medical infusion pumpCortex-MDeterminism and safety dominate. A small, auditable bare-metal or RTOS program on a Cortex-M with a watchdog and an MPU is far easier to certify than a general purpose OS, whose scheduling is non-deterministic and whose code base is too large to verify
The deciding question

Does it need a general purpose operating system? If yes — for drivers, a file system, networking or third-party applications — you need a Cortex-A with an MMU. If no, a Cortex-M gives lower power, lower cost and better determinism. Case (iii) shows that more capability can be a disadvantage: in a safety-certified device, a smaller and more predictable system is the better engineering choice.

Q12.3   Type T  ·  10 marks

Explain the Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller and why it matters in embedded design

Model answer

Definition

Nested vectored interrupt control (NVIC) is a method of prioritising interrupts, improving the MCU's performance and reducing interrupt latency. It also provides implementation schemes for handling interrupts that occur while other interrupts are being executed, or while the CPU is restoring its previous state and resuming its suspended process.

The three ideas in the name

TermMeaning
NestedA higher-priority interrupt can pre-empt a handler that is already running, rather than waiting for it to finish
VectoredEach interrupt source has its own handler address, so the CPU jumps straight to the right code instead of polling to discover the source
ControllerDedicated hardware performs the prioritisation, saving and restoring, not software

Why it matters

  1. Deterministic latency. Hardware stacking of registers on entry means a fixed, known number of cycles between the interrupt and the first instruction of the handler — essential in hard real-time systems.
  2. Correct priority under load. Without nesting, an urgent event arriving during a slow handler waits. In a drone, an IMU sample must pre-empt a telemetry transmission, not queue behind it.
  3. Tail-chaining. When one interrupt follows another, the controller moves directly from one handler to the next without unstacking and restacking, saving cycles.
  4. Late arrival handling. The deck's phrase about interrupts occurring "when the CPU is in the process of restoring its previous state" refers to exactly this — a higher-priority interrupt arriving during the return sequence is serviced immediately rather than being missed.

This is the mechanism behind "interrupt performance — required for deterministic real-time sensor acquisition" in the drone selection criteria. It is also the architectural reason a Cortex-M is preferred over an application processor in safety-critical control, where predictable latency matters more than average throughput.

Q12.4   Type S  ·  10 marks

Design a handheld toll collection device

Using the spot billing machine as a model, specify a handheld toll collection device. State the processor, memory, peripherals and power system, and justify each against the five-step sequence.

Model answer

1. Application requirement analysis

Collect tolls at a booth or roadside; accept cash, card and contactless payment; print a receipt; record every transaction with a timestamp and vehicle class; upload transactions to a central server; operate for a full shift on battery; survive outdoor use.

2. Processor architecture analysis

ARM Cortex-M4 (a small step up from the M3 of the deck's example). The workload is menu handling, printing, cryptography for card payment and modem control — no operating system required. The M4's DSP instructions accelerate the cryptographic operations that card payment needs.

3. Peripheral set analysis

RequirementPeripheral
Contactless paymentSPI or I²C to a MIFARE contactless reader
Card payment securitySecure element — the ATM case study's cryptoprocessor argument applies here
ReceiptSerial interface to a thermal or impact printer
UploadUART to a GSM/GPRS modem
Location and timeOptional GPS; RTC with battery backup
Operator entryKeypad matrix on GPIO; graphical LCD
Vehicle class captureOptional barcode or RFID reader

4. Technical analysis

Execution speed of roughly 100 MHz is ample. Operating voltage 3.3 V. Program memory 512 KB–1 MB. Non-volatile data memory of 8 MB with multi-year retention for the transaction log — the same requirement, and the same justification, as the billing machine. A 7.4 V Li-ion pack sized for a full shift.

5. Non-technical analysis

Cost must suit deployment in quantity across many booths. Software tools — a mature ARM toolchain. Package and enclosure — sealed against rain and dust for roadside use. Vendor support and long-term supply, since toll infrastructure is replaced slowly.

Conclusion and the one hard requirement

The binding constraint is transaction integrity, not performance. Every toll collected is money owed, so the transaction must be committed to non-volatile memory before the receipt prints, and the log must survive power loss and battery removal — which is why the 10-year-retention non-volatile memory of the deck's example is the specification to carry across, and why a secure element is required for card data.

Q12.5   Type S  ·  5 marks

Why does the rugged terminal specify IP65 and Gorilla glass, and what design metrics do these serve?

Model answer

What they are. IP65 means the enclosure is totally dust-tight and protected against low-pressure water jets from any direction. Corning Gorilla glass is a chemically strengthened cover glass resistant to scratches and impact. Together they let the device handle drops, bumps, spills, dust and vibration.

Design metricHow these features serve it
Correctness / reliabilityAn ingress-related failure in a warehouse is indistinguishable from a software fault to the user; sealing removes a whole class of field failures
SafetyShattered glass in a food warehouse or manufacturing line is a contamination and injury hazard
Unit costIncreased — this is a deliberate trade. The design accepts higher unit cost to reduce total cost of ownership
Size and weightWorsened — sealing gaskets and reinforcement add bulk

The environmental constraint. Module 1 lists "operate under extreme environmental conditions" among the characteristics of embedded systems. The deck's own description — built for life out in the field, for logistics, express delivery, warehousing, retail and industrial manufacture — is that characteristic made into a specification.

The economic argument to state: a consumer phone that fails is replaced by the user; a warehouse terminal that fails stops the operator working. The cost of downtime dwarfs the extra unit cost of ruggedisation, which is why the trade is worth making here and not in a consumer product.

UNIT 13

Case Study 2 — The Digital Still Camera

Module 3 · slides 26–43  ·  Types: T, S  ·  Weight: high  ·  The DSP selection case

What a digital still camera contains (slide 26)

Digital still cameras require a significant amount of silicon:

  • The sensor — CCD or CMOS
  • The analog components — ADC, NTSC encoder
  • The engine — a Digital Signal Processor
Slide 26, quotable

"DSP is the brain of the camera and is responsible for performing all the computations needed to process and compress the image."

The signal chain (slides 29–30)

  1. Most DSCs use a CCD imager to sense the images.
  2. The driver electronics and the Timing Generator circuitry generate the necessary signals to clock the CCD.
  3. Correlated Double Sampling and Automatic Gain Control electronics are used to get a good-quality image signal from the CCD sensor.
  4. This CCD data is then digitised and fed into the DSC engine.
  5. All the image-processing and image-compression operations are performed in the DSC engine.
  6. The user can view the image to be captured on the LCD display.
  7. The compressed images are stored in Flash memory.
  8. An NTSC/PAL video signal allows viewing captured and preview images on a TV monitor.
  9. Connection to an external PC or printer through an RS-232 or USB port.

Digital images and the image pipeline (slides 32, 37)

A digital image is a multidimensional array of numbers — a single number in the case of intensity images, or a vector in the case of colour images. Each component is called a pixel and associates with the pixel value.

Slide 37 — the sentence that selects the processor

"The Colour Filtered Array (CFA) data needs to undergo a significant amount of image processing before the image can be finally presented in a usable format for compression. All these processing stages are collectively called the image pipeline. Most of these tasks are multiply-accumulate (MAC) intensive operations. The TMS320C54x DSP is well suited to perform these tasks efficiently and generate a high-quality image that is close to the image quality offered by traditional film from the raw CCD data."

The chosen processor — TMS320C54x (slides 38–43)

  • The system interfaces to the CCD/CMOS module directly.
  • The DSP reads the data from the sensor, processes the raw sensor data, and writes it to the SDRAM.
  • The built-in NTSC/PAL encoder chip on the board allows direct display of the processed picture on a TV monitor.
  • All image pipeline operations, including JPEG compression, are performed on a 16 × 16 block of pixels, and the compressed bit stream is written out to SDRAM.
  • All image pipeline operations can be executed on chip since only a small 16 × 16 block is used.
  • The TMS320C549 is well suited due to its large on-chip memory — 32 K × 16-bit RAM and 16 K × 16-bit ROM.
  • Processing time is kept short because there is no need for external high-speed memory.
  • High performance (100 MIPS) at low power consumption (0.45 mA/MIPS).
  • The entire image pipeline, including JPEG, takes about 150 cycles per pixel.
  • A 1-Mpixel CCD image can be processed in 1.5 seconds on a 100 MHz TMS320C54x, giving about a 2-second shot-to-shot delay including data movement from external to on-chip memory.

Numericals

N13.1 — Verify the deck's claim that a 1-Mpixel image takes 1.5 s at 150 cycles/pixel on a 100 MHz processor.

Total cycles = 1,000,000 pixels × 150 cycles = 150,000,000 cycles Time = 150 × 10^6 / 100 × 10^6 = 1.5 seconds ✓ Shot-to-shot delay ≈ 2 s, the extra 0.5 s being data movement.

N13.2 — How long would a 5-Mpixel image take on the same processor? What clock would be needed for a 0.5 s shot-to-shot delay?

5 Mpixel: 5 × 10^6 × 150 = 750 × 10^6 cycles = 750 / 100 = 7.5 seconds — unacceptably slow For 0.5 s: required rate = 750 × 10^6 / 0.5 = 1500 MHz This is why real cameras use dedicated ASIC image processors rather than a general DSP as resolution rises.

N13.3 — Compute the current drawn by the TMS320C549 at full 100 MIPS, and the energy for one 1-Mpixel image.

Current = 100 MIPS × 0.45 mA/MIPS = 45 mA At 3.3 V: power = 3.3 × 0.045 = 148.5 mW Energy per image = 148.5 mW × 1.5 s = 0.223 J From a 5 Wh battery: 5 × 3600 / 0.223 = ~80,000 images (processing only — sensor, LCD and Flash dominate in practice)

N13.4 — Why is the pipeline run on 16 × 16 blocks, and how much on-chip memory does one block need?

Block = 16 × 16 = 256 pixels Colour, 3 components at 16 bits = 256 × 3 × 2 = 1536 bytes On-chip RAM = 32K × 16-bit = 64 KB A block plus working buffers fits easily on chip, so "all image pipeline operations can be executed on chip" and no external high-speed memory is needed. 16 x 16 is also the JPEG minimum coded unit for 4:2:0 chroma.

Theory and situation questions

Q13.1   Type T  ·  10 marks

Explain the architecture of a digital still camera and justify the choice of a DSP

Model answer

Introduction

A digital still camera requires significant silicon content: the sensor (CCD or CMOS), the analog components (ADC, NTSC encoder) and the engine, which is a DSP. The DSP is the brain of the camera, responsible for performing all the computations needed to process and compress the image.

Block diagram and signal chain

(Draw the chain and give the nine numbered steps above.)

The image pipeline

The Colour Filtered Array data from the sensor must undergo significant processing before it can be compressed. These stages collectively are the image pipeline, and typically include colour interpolation, white balance, colour correction, gamma correction and sharpening.

Why a DSP — the deciding argument

Most of the image pipeline tasks are multiply-accumulate intensive operations. A DSP's datapath is built for exactly this: a single-cycle MAC unit, multiple memory buses so coefficients and data are fetched simultaneously, hardware loops and saturating arithmetic. A general purpose processor performing the same convolution would need several instructions per MAC.

Why the TMS320C549 specifically

AttributeValueWhy it matters
On-chip memory32 K × 16 RAM, 16 K × 16 ROMThe whole pipeline runs on chip on a 16 × 16 block, so no external high-speed memory is needed and processing time stays short
Performance100 MIPS150 cycles/pixel × 1 Mpixel = 1.5 s per image
Power0.45 mA/MIPS45 mA at full rate — acceptable in a battery-powered camera
IntegrationInterfaces to the CCD/CMOS module directly; built-in NTSC/PAL encoderFewer external components, lower cost and size

Result

The entire image pipeline including JPEG takes about 150 cycles per pixel, so a 1-Mpixel image is processed in 1.5 seconds, giving roughly a 2-second shot-to-shot delay once data movement is included.

Q13.2   Type S  ·  10 marks

Scale the camera design to 12 megapixels and 30 frames per second video

Analyse whether the TMS320C549 remains suitable, and recommend an alternative architecture.

Model answer

The arithmetic

Verdict

The TMS320C549 is unsuitable by a very large margin. Even the still case at 18 seconds per photograph is commercially impossible, and the video case is 540 times beyond its capability.

What changes architecturally

ProblemSolution
MAC throughputA dedicated ASIC image signal processor (ISP) with hard-wired pipeline stages. Fixed-function silicon performs colour interpolation, white balance and sharpening in parallel at pixel rate rather than sequentially in software
CompressionA hardware JPEG/H.264 encoder block rather than software compression
MemoryA 12 Mpixel frame no longer fits on chip. External DDR SDRAM with a wide bus and DMA is mandatory — the C549's key advantage of running entirely on chip is lost
Data movementDMA engines so the CPU is not the bottleneck moving pixels
ControlAn ARM application processor alongside the ISP for the user interface, file system and connectivity

The design-metric argument

This is a move from a programmable DSP to an ASIC, and it follows Module 1's rule exactly: the image pipeline is fixed for the product's life and camera volumes are very high, so the ASIC's high NRE cost is amortised and its highest performance and best power efficiency are exactly what a battery-powered camera needs.

The general lesson: as a workload's throughput requirement grows by orders of magnitude, the correct response is not a faster processor of the same kind but a change of implementation technology. This is the deck's slide-77 spectrum being traversed under pressure of a new requirement.

Q13.3   Type T  ·  10 marks

Explain the image pipeline and why it is MAC intensive

Model answer

What the pipeline is

Raw data from the sensor is Colour Filtered Array (CFA) data — each photosite records only one colour, because a colour filter mosaic covers the sensor. This data needs to undergo a significant amount of image processing before the image can be presented in a usable format for compression. Those stages collectively are the image pipeline.

Typical stages

StageWhat it doesOperation type
CFA interpolationReconstructs the two missing colours at every pixel from neighboursWeighted sum of neighbours = MAC
White balanceCorrects for the colour of the illuminant so white appears whitePer-channel multiply
Colour balance / correctionMaps sensor colour space to display colour space3 × 3 matrix multiply per pixel = 9 MACs
Gamma correctionApplies the display transfer functionTable lookup
Kernel operations — sharpening, noise filteringConvolution with a small kernelN × N MACs per pixel
JPEG compressionDCT, quantisation, entropy coding on 16 × 16 blocksDCT is entirely MAC

Why this is MAC intensive

Every stage except gamma is a weighted sum — each output pixel is a sum of input pixels multiplied by coefficients. That is the definition of multiply-accumulate. A 3 × 3 convolution costs nine MACs per pixel per channel; the DCT costs dozens more. Summed across the pipeline this reaches the deck's figure of about 150 cycles per pixel.

Why a DSP suits it

A DSP provides a single-cycle MAC unit, multiple memory buses so the coefficient and the pixel are fetched simultaneously, hardware loop control with no per-iteration branch overhead, and saturating arithmetic so overflow clips rather than wraps — which for image data means a highlight stays white instead of turning black.

This is why the deck states that the TMS320C54x "is well suited to perform these tasks efficiently and generate a high-quality image that is close to the image quality offered by traditional film from the raw CCD data".

Q13.4   Type S  ·  10 marks

Design the processing subsystem for an agricultural crop-imaging camera

A drone-mounted camera must capture multispectral images, compute a vegetation index per pixel on board, and transmit only the results. Select the processing architecture and justify.

Model answer

Requirement analysis

Four spectral bands at 2 Mpixel each, captured every second while flying. A vegetation index such as NDVI is computed per pixel as (NIR − Red)/(NIR + Red). Only the resulting index map and statistics are transmitted, because the telemetry link cannot carry raw imagery.

The arithmetic

Architecture

ElementChoiceJustification
Sensor front endMultispectral CMOS with on-chip ADCCMOS integrates the ADC, reducing the analog component count relative to CCD
Image pipelineHardware ISP in an SoC1200 MIPS of MAC work is beyond a software DSP at acceptable power; fixed-function silicon does it at pixel rate
Index computationDSP or GPU/NPU blockSimple, massively parallel per-pixel arithmetic — ideal for SIMD
Control and commsARM Cortex-A with LinuxFile system, telemetry stack, mission logic
StorageSD cardRaw imagery retained for later analysis; matches the drone answer of Unit 11
Link to flight controllerUART or CANPosition tagging from the STM32F4 so each image carries GPS coordinates

The key design decision

Process on board and transmit only results. Raw multispectral imagery at 8 MB per frame cannot cross a LoRa or Wi-Fi telemetry link in one second, whereas an index map plus statistics is kilobytes. Moving the computation to the sensor rather than the data to the computer is what makes the system feasible — a decision driven entirely by the communication constraint, not by the processing constraint.

Note the two-processor split: the flight controller stays a Cortex-M4 for determinism, while the camera payload uses a Cortex-A with an ISP for throughput. They communicate over a serial link. Different binding constraints in the same aircraft produce different processors — which is exactly the point of the Module 3 framework.

Q13.5   Type S  ·  5 marks

Why does the camera process the image in 16 × 16 blocks rather than whole frames?

Model answer

The memory argument — the deck's own reasoning. "All image pipeline operations can be executed on chip since only a small 16 × 16 block of the image is used. The TMS320C549 is well suited due to its large on-chip memory (32 K × 16-bit RAM and 16 K × 16-bit ROM). In this way, the processing time is kept short, because there is no need for external high-speed memory."

ApproachMemory neededConsequence
Whole 1-Mpixel frame~3 MB for colourMust live in external SDRAM; every pipeline stage re-reads it, so the processor stalls on memory
16 × 16 block~1.5 KBFits in the 64 KB on-chip RAM; every stage operates at full speed with no external access

The second reason: JPEG. A 16 × 16 block is the minimum coded unit for JPEG with 4:2:0 chroma subsampling, so the pipeline block size matches the compression block size and no re-blocking is needed between stages.

The general principle: keep the working set inside on-chip memory. On-chip access is several times faster than external SDRAM and consumes far less energy, so choosing a block size that fits on chip converts a memory-bound problem into a compute-bound one. The same principle appears as cache blocking in general purpose computing.

UNIT 14

Case Study 3 — The ATM

Module 3 · slides 44–48  ·  Types: T, S  ·  Weight: medium  ·  The security-driven selection

Definition (slide 44)

Slide 44, quotable

"An automated teller machine (ATM) is a computerised telecommunications device that provides a financial institution's customers a secure method of performing financial transactions in a public space without the need for a human clerk or bank teller."

Two phrases set every design decision: "secure" and "in a public space". The machine is physically accessible to attackers, so security is a hardware problem, not merely a software one.

Hardware (slide 46)

ComponentPurpose
CPUTo control the user interface and transaction devices
Magnetic and/or chip card readerTo identify the customer
PIN padSimilar in layout to a touch-tone or calculator keypad, often manufactured as part of a secure enclosure
Secure cryptoprocessorGenerally within a secure enclosure
DisplayUsed by the customer for performing the transaction
Function key buttons or touchscreenUsually close to the display, to select aspects of the transaction
Record printerTo provide the customer with a record of their transaction
VaultTo store the parts of the machinery requiring restricted access
HousingFor aesthetics and to attach signage

Inside the vault (slide 47)

  • Dispensing mechanism — to provide cash or other items of value
  • Deposit mechanism — to take items of value from the customer
  • Security sensors — magnetic, thermal, seismic
  • Locks — to ensure controlled access to the contents of the vault

Why three sensor types: each detects a different attack. Magnetic detects tools and drills; thermal detects cutting torches; seismic detects hammering and explosive attack. Defence in depth — no single sensor covers all attack methods.

Networking (slide 48)

The internet service provider (ISP) plays an important role: it provides communication between the ATM and host processors. When a transaction is made, the details are input by the cardholder; this information is passed on to the host processor by the ATM; the host processor checks these details with an authorised bank; and if the details match, the host processor sends the approval code to the machine so that the cash can be transferred.

Theory and situation questions

Q14.1   Type T  ·  10 marks

Explain the architecture and working of an ATM, and justify its processor selection

Model answer

Definition and block diagram

(Quote slide 44, then draw slide 45: card reader, PIN pad, display and function keys as inputs; the CPU at the centre; the secure cryptoprocessor alongside it inside the secure enclosure; printer, dispenser and deposit mechanism as outputs; the network interface to the ISP; and the vault containing the dispensing and deposit mechanisms, security sensors and locks.)

Hardware

(Give the nine-row hardware table and the four vault items.)

Working

(Give the transaction flow: card and PIN entered, details passed to the host processor via the ISP, host checks with the authorised bank, approval code returned, cash dispensed, receipt printed.)

Processor selection and justification

CriterionJustification
SecurityThe binding constraint. A separate secure cryptoprocessor within a secure enclosure handles PIN encryption and key storage, so keys never appear in the main CPU's memory. The PIN pad is itself part of a secure enclosure
Processing speedModest — the workload is a user interface and a transaction protocol, not computation. The main CPU only controls the user interface and transaction devices
Operating systemRequired for the network stack, file system and GUI; therefore an application-class processor with an MMU
Communication interfacesEthernet or leased line to the ISP; serial to the card reader, printer and dispenser
ReliabilityWatchdog and fault detection; a hung ATM holding a customer's card is a serious failure
Non-volatile storageTransaction journal that must survive power loss — every dispense is money
EnvironmentalOperates unattended in a public space, often outdoors
Long-term supplyATMs are deployed for a decade or more; vendor support and part availability matter

Conclusion

Unlike the drone or the camera, the ATM is not selected by performance. A general purpose CPU of modest speed is sufficient, but it must be paired with a dedicated secure cryptoprocessor. The security requirement, not the computational requirement, shapes the architecture — which is why the deck lists the cryptoprocessor as a distinct hardware component rather than a software library.

Q14.2   Type S  ·  10 marks

Why is a separate cryptoprocessor used instead of running encryption on the main CPU?

Model answer
ReasonExplanation
Physical key isolationEncryption keys are generated and stored inside the secure enclosure and never leave it. Even full compromise of the main CPU's software cannot read them, because they were never in its memory
Tamper responseA secure cryptoprocessor erases its keys when the enclosure is opened, drilled or subjected to abnormal temperature or voltage. A general CPU has no such mechanism
The PIN never appears in clearThe PIN pad is manufactured as part of a secure enclosure and is wired directly to the cryptoprocessor, which encrypts it at the point of entry. The main CPU handles only an encrypted PIN block
CertificationPayment standards require certified secure hardware. A general purpose CPU running a general purpose OS cannot be certified, because its attack surface is unbounded
Side-channel resistanceCryptoprocessors are designed against timing, power-analysis and electromagnetic attacks. Software encryption on a general CPU leaks key material through execution time and power draw
Public space exposureThe deck's definition stresses transactions in a public space. The attacker has unlimited physical access, so the threat model includes opening the machine
The principle to state

Separate what must be trusted from what must be large. The main CPU is large, complex and impossible to fully verify. The cryptoprocessor is small, single-purpose and can be exhaustively audited and physically protected. Shrinking the trusted computing base to something verifiable is the core of secure system design.

Where else this appears in the course: the toll-collection device's secure element and the spot billing machine's password protection follow the same reasoning, and Module 1's safety metric — the probability the system will not cause harm — is the design metric being optimised.

Q14.3   Type S  ·  10 marks

Design the security subsystem for a cash-in-transit deposit safe

Using the ATM's vault as a model, specify sensors, processor and communications for an in-store safe that accepts cash deposits and reports to a central monitoring service.

Model answer

Requirements

Accept and validate banknotes; credit the deposit to a store account; resist physical attack; report status and alarms to a monitoring centre; log every event non-volatilely; continue working through a power cut.

Sensors — following the ATM vault model

SensorAttack detected
MagneticDrilling and tool contact
ThermalCutting torch or thermal lance
Seismic / vibrationHammering, prying, explosive attack
Door position and lock stateUnauthorised opening
Tilt / movementRemoval of the whole safe
Enclosure tamper switchAccess to the electronics

Processor and memory

Cortex-M4 microcontroller — the workload is sensor monitoring, note validation control and a communications protocol, not computation. Add a secure element for authentication keys, following the ATM cryptoprocessor argument. Memory: 512 KB Flash; 64 KB SRAM; non-volatile event log with multi-year retention.

Communications and power

Ethernet as the primary link with GSM as a backup, because an attacker's first act is to cut the network. A battery backup keeps sensors, logging and the radio alive through a mains cut — power removal must not disable the alarm.

The critical design decisions

  1. Sensors and alarm reporting run from battery-backed power. Otherwise cutting the mains disarms the safe.
  2. Heartbeat rather than alarm-only reporting. The monitoring centre expects a message every few minutes; silence is itself an alarm, so cutting the link cannot suppress detection.
  3. Events written to non-volatile memory before acting, so the log survives power loss mid-transaction — the same integrity requirement as the vending machine and the toll device.
  4. Independent hardwired alarm path that does not depend on the microcontroller, so a hung or compromised processor cannot suppress the siren. This mirrors the traffic system's hardwired failsafe.
  5. Defence in depth — multiple sensor types because no single one covers all attack methods.

Binding constraint: security under conditions where the attacker controls power, network and physical access. Every decision above follows from assuming the attacker removes something you depend on.

Q14.4   Type S  ·  5 marks

Compare the binding constraint of the three Module 3 case studies

Model answer
Case studyBinding constraintProcessor chosenWhy that constraint selects that processor
Handheld spot billing machineBattery life, cost and peripheralsARM Cortex-M3, 120 MHzDeveloped for high-performance, low-cost platforms; runs a fixed application with no OS, sleeping between keystrokes
Digital still cameraMAC throughputTMS320C54x DSPThe image pipeline is multiply-accumulate intensive; large on-chip memory keeps the 16 × 16 block on chip at 100 MIPS and 0.45 mA/MIPS
ATMSecurityGeneral purpose CPU + secure cryptoprocessorPerformance is modest, but transactions occur in a public space, so keys must live in tamper-responding hardware
The single lesson of Module 3

The binding constraint picks the processor. Three products, three completely different processor classes, and in no case was "which is fastest?" the deciding question. Identify what the application cannot compromise on — power, throughput, determinism or security — and the selection follows.

Extend the pattern to the CAT answer: the agricultural drone's binding constraint is real-time determinism with floating-point mathematics at low power, which selects the Cortex-M4. Adding that fourth row to this table is a strong way to close a Module 3 answer.

Q14.5   Type S  ·  10 marks

Design an unmanned petrol pump payment terminal

Combining the ATM and handheld case studies, specify a self-service fuel payment terminal. Give the block diagram, working, processor and memory selection, and the security measures.

Model answer

Block diagram

Working

  1. The customer inserts or taps a card; the reader passes the card data to the CPU.
  2. The PIN is entered on a keypad that is part of a secure enclosure and is encrypted at the point of entry by the cryptoprocessor.
  3. The encrypted PIN block and card details are sent through the network to the host processor, which checks with the authorised bank.
  4. On approval a pre-authorisation hold is placed and the pump controller is enabled.
  5. The customer dispenses fuel; the pump controller reports the volume delivered.
  6. The final amount is captured against the pre-authorisation, the transaction is written to non-volatile memory before the receipt prints, and the receipt is issued.

Processor and memory

Main CPU: an ARM Cortex-A class application processor running Linux — required for the touchscreen GUI, network stack, payment application and file system. Cryptoprocessor: a certified secure element in a tamper-responding enclosure. Memory: 512 MB–1 GB DRAM; 4–8 GB eMMC for OS and logs; a small non-volatile store for the transaction journal.

Security measures

  • Keys never leave the secure enclosure; the main CPU sees only encrypted PIN blocks.
  • Tamper detection on the card reader slot to counter skimming devices — the attack this class of terminal actually suffers.
  • Physical enclosure sensors following the ATM vault model.
  • Heartbeat reporting so a severed network link raises an alarm.
  • Transaction integrity — commit to non-volatile memory before dispensing fuel, so a power cut cannot deliver fuel that was never billed.

The distinctive risk here, absent from the ATM, is that the goods are dispensed after authorisation and in a variable quantity — which is why the pre-authorisation hold followed by final capture is the correct transaction model, and why the pump controller must be an independent subsystem that cannot be enabled without an approval code.

UNIT 15

Special Purpose Processors and Integrated Design

Module 3 · slide 49 + synthesis  ·  Types: T, S  ·  Weight: high  ·  Everything combined

Single-purpose processors (slide 49)

Slide 49, quotable

"Using a single-purpose processor in an embedded system results in several design metric benefits and drawbacks, which are essentially the inverse of those for general purpose processors."

Benefits: "Performance may be fast, size and power may be small, and unit-cost may be low for large quantities."

Drawbacks: "Design time and NRE costs may be high, flexibility is low, unit cost may be high for small quantities, and performance may not match general-purpose processors for some applications."

MetricSingle-purpose processorGeneral purpose processor
PerformanceMay be fastLower for the specific task
SizeMay be smallLarger
PowerMay be smallLarger
Unit cost, large quantityLowHigher
Unit cost, small quantityHighLower
Design timeHighLow
NRE costHighLow
FlexibilityLowHigh

Note the last drawback carefully: "performance may not match general-purpose processors for some applications". A single-purpose processor is faster only at its task; on anything else it may be useless. That asymmetry is the whole reason the choice is application-driven.

How to attack any selection question

Name the binding constraintPower, throughput, determinism, security or cost. State it in the opening paragraph — every later choice must trace back to it.

Draw the block diagramSensors left, processor centre, actuators and comms right, power and memory below. Three of the ten marks.

Describe the workingFour to six numbered steps tracing data through that diagram.

Name a real processor and give a spec tableCore, clock, FPU, timers/PWM, interfaces, reliability features. Naming a real part is worth more than saying "a suitable microcontroller".

Split the memory four waysFlash for firmware · SRAM for run-time data · EEPROM for calibration · external storage for logging.

Fill the ten-row criteria tableCriterion and justification. Match the answer key's density.

Close by excluding an alternative"An ATmega328P would be inadequate because…" Showing what you rejected and why proves the choice was reasoned.

Integrated questions

Q15.1   Type T  ·  10 marks

Compare single-purpose and general purpose processors across the design metrics

Model answer

(Give the eight-row inverse table, then the analysis below.)

Why the relationship is an inversion

A general purpose processor must handle any program, so its hardware carries instruction decoding, general registers and control logic that a given application mostly does not use. That generality costs die area, power and cycles on every instruction.

A single-purpose processor implements only the required function in hardware. Nothing is decoded, nothing is fetched, nothing is general. The result is fast, small and low power — but it can do nothing else, and every change requires redesigning silicon.

The cost crossover

This is why the deck states unit cost is low for large quantities but high for small quantities — the same NRE divided by a small volume dominates the per-unit figure.

Conclusion

Neither is superior. The choice is set by volume and by whether the function will change — exactly the two-question test from the GPP/ASIP/ASIC comparison of Module 1.

Q15.2   Type S  ·  10 marks

Select processor and memory for a smart electricity meter

The meter measures voltage and current, computes energy, displays consumption, stores 12 months of billing data, communicates with the utility over GPRS, and detects tampering. Draw a block diagram and justify.

Model answer

Binding constraints: 15-year unattended reliability, tamper resistance and unit cost at very high volume.

Working

  1. Voltage and current are sampled simultaneously at several kHz by a high-resolution ADC.
  2. The processor computes instantaneous power as the product, and integrates it to obtain energy in kWh.
  3. Cumulative energy is written to non-volatile memory at intervals, with a tariff-slot breakdown.
  4. The display shows current consumption; the GPRS modem uploads readings to the utility.
  5. Tamper sensors — magnetic field, cover opening, reverse current — are monitored continuously and logged with a timestamp from the battery-backed RTC.

Selection

CriterionJustification
ADC resolutionThe critical specification. Current must be measured accurately over a wide dynamic range, from standby loads of a few watts to several kilowatts. A 16 or 24-bit sigma-delta ADC is required; a 10-bit ADC cannot resolve small loads
Processing speedModest — multiply and accumulate at a few kHz. A Cortex-M0+ or M3 class core suffices
DSP blockOptional hardware metering engine computes RMS and power factor without CPU load
FlashFirmware plus the GPRS protocol stack
Non-volatile data12 months of billing data that must survive power cuts — the deck's spot billing machine specifies 10-year retention for the same reason
RTC with backupTime-of-use tariffs require accurate time even through outages
CommunicationUART to the GPRS modem
ReliabilityWatchdog; the meter is unattended for 15 years
Power consumptionThe meter's own consumption is not billable to the customer, so it must be minimal
Unit costMillions of units — this is the classic case where an ASIC or highly integrated metering SoC is justified

Conclusion

A dedicated metering SoC — effectively a single-purpose processor with an integrated Cortex-M core — is the right answer. The function is fixed for the product's life and the volume is in millions, so the high NRE is amortised to nothing while the low unit cost, small size and low power are exactly the benefits slide 49 attributes to a single-purpose processor.

Q15.3   Type S  ·  10 marks

Select processor and memory for an autonomous warehouse robot

The robot navigates by LiDAR and cameras, avoids obstacles, lifts shelves, and coordinates with a fleet server. Justify the architecture.

Model answer

Binding constraint: two incompatible requirements in one machine — perception needs throughput, motion control needs determinism. The correct answer is a split architecture, not a single processor.

DomainProcessorWhy
Perception and planningCortex-A with GPU/NPU, running Linux and ROSLiDAR point clouds and camera frames are massively parallel data. Needs a file system, networking and mapping libraries — therefore an OS and an MMU
Motion control and safetyCortex-M4Wheel control loops at hundreds of hertz with deterministic latency. Watchdog and emergency stop must work even if the Linux side crashes
CriterionJustification
Processing speedPerception: billions of operations/s. Control: modest but strictly periodic
Floating pointBoth — SLAM on the A core, PID on the M core's FPU
Timers / PWMOn the M core: wheel motors, lift actuator
Interrupt performanceNVIC on the M core for encoder and emergency-stop inputs
MemoryA core: 2–4 GB DRAM for point clouds. M core: 192 KB SRAM for control state
External storageSSD or eMMC for maps and operational logs
CommunicationWi-Fi to the fleet server; CAN or UART between the two processors
PowerBattery-powered; the A core sleeps or throttles when stationary
ReliabilityThe M core holds a hardware emergency stop independent of the A core, plus a watchdog on both
EnvironmentWarehouse: dust, vibration, wide temperature

Why the split is the answer

Running motion control on the Linux processor would make stopping distance depend on scheduler behaviour — unacceptable near people. Running perception on the Cortex-M is impossible for throughput reasons. Two binding constraints in one machine require two processors, each selected by its own constraint, communicating over a defined interface.

The safety argument to close on: the emergency stop is wired to the M core and to a hardware relay, so it functions even if the perception processor has crashed — the same principle as the traffic system's hardwired failsafe and the deposit safe's independent alarm path.

Q15.4   Type S  ·  10 marks

Select processor and memory for a portable patient monitor

The monitor measures ECG, SpO₂ and blood pressure, displays waveforms, alarms on abnormal readings, stores 24 hours of data and transmits to a nursing station.

Model answer

Binding constraint: safety-critical reliability with real-time signal processing on battery. An alarm that fails to sound, or a waveform that freezes, endangers a patient.

Working

  1. ECG electrodes feed a high-gain instrumentation amplifier and a 24-bit ADC sampling at 500 Hz per lead.
  2. SpO₂ is measured by alternately pulsing red and infrared LEDs and sampling a photodiode; the ratio of absorptions gives oxygen saturation.
  3. Blood pressure is measured on demand by the oscillometric method — inflate, deflate, detect pulse oscillations.
  4. The processor filters the ECG to remove mains interference and baseline wander, detects QRS complexes and computes heart rate.
  5. Waveforms are drawn on the display; readings outside limits raise audible and visual alarms.
  6. 24 hours of trend data is stored locally and transmitted to the nursing station over Wi-Fi.
CriterionJustification
Processing speedContinuous digital filtering on three signals plus waveform rendering — a Cortex-M4 or M7 at 100–200 MHz
DSP instructions / FPUECG filtering and QRS detection are MAC-intensive; the M4's DSP extensions handle this without a separate DSP
ADC resolution24-bit external ADC — an ECG signal is about 1 mV riding on much larger offsets, so a 10 or 12-bit converter cannot resolve it. Same argument as the weighing machine's HX711
Interrupt performanceDeterministic sampling; jitter distorts the waveform and corrupts heart-rate calculation
Flash512 KB–1 MB for firmware, filters and the alarm logic
SRAM256 KB for waveform buffers and the display frame buffer
External storage24 hours of trend data — SD card or serial Flash
PowerBattery-powered and portable; must survive transport between wards
ReliabilityWatchdog is mandatory. A frozen monitor showing a stale waveform is more dangerous than a blank one, so the watchdog must reset into a state that alarms rather than one that looks normal
CertificationMedical device standards favour a small, auditable bare-metal or certified-RTOS system on a Cortex-M over a general purpose OS

Why not an application processor

A Cortex-A running Linux would render nicer graphics but introduces non-deterministic scheduling and a code base far too large to certify. In a safety-critical device, a smaller and more predictable system is the better engineering choice — the same conclusion reached for the infusion pump in Unit 12.

The design-metric framing: the dominant metrics are safety — the probability the system will not cause harm — and correctness, with power close behind. Performance and unit cost are subordinate, which is the inverse of the consumer products elsewhere in this course.

Q15.5   Type S  ·  10 marks

A single company must build three products on one platform

A firm makes a smart doorbell, a security camera and a home hub. Recommend whether to use one processor family across all three, and justify in terms of design metrics.

Model answer

The three products analysed

ProductBinding constraintProcessor class
Smart doorbellBattery life; wakes on motion, streams brieflyCortex-M with a wake-capable camera, or a low-end A core
Security cameraContinuous video encoding; mains poweredCortex-A with a hardware video encoder
Home hubMultiple radio protocols, always on, runs applicationsCortex-A with Linux

Recommendation: one family, not one part

Standardise on the ARM architecture across all three, but use different family members: a Cortex-M class part for the doorbell and Cortex-A class parts for the camera and hub.

Design metricEffect of a common architecture
NRE costReduced sharply. One toolchain, one debugger, one set of engineering skills, and shared driver and application code across three products
Time-to-marketReduced. The second and third products reuse proven code and build infrastructure
Unit costOptimised per product, because each uses the smallest family member that meets its requirement. Forcing one part across all three would over-specify the doorbell and under-specify the hub
PowerOptimised per product — the doorbell gets a deep-sleep M core rather than an always-on A core
FlexibilityHigh — a product can move up or down the family as requirements evolve, with the same skills
CorrectnessImproved — shared, repeatedly exercised code is better tested than three separate code bases

Why one single part would be wrong

Using the hub's Cortex-A in the doorbell would destroy its battery life and raise its unit cost for capability it never uses. Using the doorbell's Cortex-M in the hub would make it unable to run Linux or handle multiple radio stacks. Standardising on the architecture captures the NRE and time-to-market savings, while selecting different family members preserves the per-product optimisation of power and unit cost.

This is the ARM partnership model paying off in practice: one instruction set, one ecosystem, an enormous range of implementations from many vendors — exactly the advantage identified in Unit 9.

Key Points, Frameworks and Traps

Everything that earns or loses marks, gathered in one place

The three frameworks you must be able to write from memory

Framework 1 — the design process (Module 1, Unit 3)

Requirements → Specification → Architecture → Components → System Integration

Goals throughout: manufacturing cost, performance, power consumption. At every step: analyse, refine, verify. Requirements are functional (output as a function of input) or non-functional (performance, cost, size, weight, power).

Framework 2 — the ten design metrics (Module 1, Unit 4)

Unit cost · NRE cost · Size · Performance · Power · Flexibility · Time-to-market · Time-to-prototype · Correctness · Safety

A design metric is a measurable feature of a system's implementation. The key design challenge is to simultaneously optimise numerous design metrics.

Framework 3 — processor selection (Module 3, Unit 11)

Four opening questions: suitable implementation? · sufficient performance? · operating system support? · adequate tools?

Five-step sequence: Application requirement → Processor architecture → Peripheral set → Technical → Non-technical

Deck contradictions — how to answer

Four places the slides disagree with themselves or with reality
IssueThe conflictAnswer with
8051 ROM sizeSlide 80 says 64 K on-chip; slide 93 says 4 KB4 KB on-chip, addressable to 64 KB externally
8051 architectureSlide 79 says Harvard; slide 123 says Von NeumannHarvard — slide 79 is correct
ARM architectureSlide 123 says modified HarvardTrue of ARM9 and Cortex. ARM7 itself is Von Neumann — one D[31:0] bus. Say which you mean
µP/µC pairingSlide 59 pairs µP with Von Neumann+RISC and µC with Harvard+CISCReproduce the table as given, but note it is a generalisation — AVR and PIC are Harvard RISC

The ten traps that cost the most marks

#TrapFix
1Writing prose before drawing the diagramThe diagram is 3–4 marks and takes 2 minutes. Draw it first
2Omitting the Justification heading in a design answerThe official key ends Q2 with it. Defend the cheap choice, then the expensive one
3Giving a component list without a justification columnThree columns: Component | Choice | Justification
4Saying "a suitable microcontroller"Name a real part — ATmega328P, Cortex-M4, STM32F4, TMS320C549
5Not splitting requirements into functional and non-functionalLabel them explicitly; the deck defines both
6Confusing requirements with specificationRequirements are informal from the customer; a specification is measurable and is the contract
7Confusing NRE cost with unit costNRE is paid once and divided by volume; unit cost is paid every time
8Claiming "faster is better"That is the general purpose criterion. Embedded selection asks for sufficient performance at least cost and power
9Ignoring memory typeSplit four ways: Flash for firmware, SRAM for run-time, EEPROM for calibration, external for logging
10Not stating the binding constraintOpen every selection answer by naming it — power, throughput, determinism, security or cost

The sentences that lift a design answer

Reusable across almost any question in these two modules
  1. "The binding constraint of this application is [X], and every selection below follows from it."
  2. "An ATmega328P would be inadequate here because it has no FPU, runs at 16 MHz and offers only 2 KB of SRAM."
  3. "NRE cost is paid once and divided by the volume; unit cost is paid every time — so high volume justifies an ASIC and low volume never does."
  4. "The calibration constants are stored in EEPROM so they survive power-off."
  5. "A watchdog timer is required because the system operates unattended and must recover from a hang."
  6. "The load cell produces about 10 mV full scale against the internal ADC's 4.88 mV step, spanning only two counts — hence the external HX711."
  7. "This is a hard real-time requirement: a late correct answer is a wrong answer."

Glossary

Every term from Modules 1 and 3, defined for an exam answer

TermDefinition
ACVMAutomatic Chocolate Vending Machine — the deck's worked case study of the full design process
ADASAdvanced Driver-Assistance Systems — uses DSPs for radar and lidar signal processing
Architecture (design stage)The plan for the overall structure of the system; describes the implementation, where the specification describes only the functions
ART AcceleratorAdaptive Real-Time accelerator — allows zero-wait-state execution from Flash on STM32 parts
ASICApplication-Specific Integrated Circuit — custom hardware for one fixed application; highest performance and best power efficiency, no flexibility, volume-sensitive cost
ASIPApplication-Specific Instruction-set Processor — designed for a class of applications; datapath optimised by adding special functional units and eliminating unused ones
Banked registersMode-specific ARM registers substituted automatically on a mode change; FIQ banks r8–r14, giving fast interrupt response
Barrel shifterARM datapath unit preprocessing Rm before the ALU; provides LSL, LSR, ASR, ROR and RRX at no extra cycle
big.LITTLEARM configuration pairing high-performance and high-efficiency cores; the Cortex-A53 can be used in one
Bottom-up designStart with components to build a system
CCDCharge-Coupled Device — the image sensor used by most digital still cameras
CFAColour Filtered Array — raw sensor data in which each photosite records one colour; must be interpolated by the image pipeline
CISCComplex Instruction Set Computing — variable-length instructions that may operate on memory; the 8051 and x86
CPLDComplex Programmable Logic Device — programmable logic for simple, fast control logic and glue logic
Correlated Double SamplingAnalog technique used with AGC to obtain a good-quality image signal from a CCD sensor
Cortex-AARM application-processor family with an MMU, able to run Linux or Android
Cortex-MARM microcontroller family with an MPU and NVIC, developed for high-performance low-cost platforms
CPSRCurrent Program Status Register — condition flags N Z C V, interrupt bits I and F, Thumb bit T, mode bits M[4:0]
CryptoprocessorSecure processor inside a tamper-responding enclosure, holding keys that never reach the main CPU
Design metricA measurable feature of a system's implementation
DeterministicExecution behaviour whose timing is predictable; required for hard real-time systems
DMIPSDhrystone MIPS — a performance measure; the Cortex-M3 example gives 150 DMIPS at 1.25 DMIPS/MHz
DSPDigital Signal Processor — specialised for real-time signal processing; used for computation-intensive work such as image processing and voice-to-text
Event triggeredActivated by an external event, typically an interrupt
FPGAField-Programmable Gate Array — reconfigurable hardware with no NRE cost; ideal for prototyping
Functional requirementThe needed output as a function of input
GPOSGeneral Purpose Operating System
GPPGeneral Purpose Processor — excellent flexibility, no hardware design effort, higher power
GPRSPacket data service over GSM; used by the spot billing machine for remote billing
GPUGraphics Processing Unit — massively parallel SIMD processor for vector and matrix operations
Hard real-timeA missed deadline causes total system failure; a late correct answer is a wrong answer
Harvard architectureSeparate program and data memories with separate buses, allowing simultaneous fetch and data access
HX71124-bit ADC with an integrated gain amplifier, designed for load cells; the CAT Q2 answer
Image pipelineThe collective processing stages converting CFA data into a compressible image; MAC intensive
In-System ProgrammingReprogramming a device in its final circuit; enables field firmware upgrade
IP65Enclosure rating — dust-tight and protected against low-pressure water jets
Load-store architectureOnly load and store instructions access memory; all data processing is register to register
MACMultiply-Accumulate — the dominant operation in signal and image processing
MCS-51Intel's name for the 8051 family, developed in 1980
MMU / MPUMemory Management Unit provides virtual memory (needed by Linux); Memory Protection Unit provides isolation only
Modified HarvardSeparate instruction and data caches over a unified main memory; ARM9 onward
NRE costNon-Recurring Engineering — the monetary cost of designing the system; paid once, then divided by the volume
Non-functional requirementPerformance, cost, physical size, weight and power consumption
NVICNested Vectored Interrupt Controller — prioritises interrupts, improves performance and reduces interrupt latency
PSPParallel Slave Port — makes the PIC appear as an addressable 8-bit peripheral on a host bus
RequirementsInformal descriptions gathered from the customer
RISCReduced Instruction Set Computing — fixed-length instructions, load-store, near one instruction per cycle
RTOSReal-Time Operating System — provides scheduling guarantees; appears from the third generation onward
SBMSpot Billing Machine — the deck's GPRS-enabled handheld case study
Single-purpose processorFast, small, low power, low unit cost at volume; but high NRE, low flexibility, high unit cost at low volume
SoCSystem on Chip — processor, memory and peripherals on one die; characteristic of fourth-generation systems
Soft real-timeA missed deadline degrades quality but the system remains useful
SpecificationRequirements refined into a measurable form; the contract between the customers and the architects
System integrationThe stage where components are combined and where bugs are typically found; debug a few modules at a time
ThumbARM's 16-bit instruction encoding, giving high code density
Time triggeredActivated by a fixed clock schedule; suits periodic sampling and control loops
Time-to-marketTime to design and manufacture to the point the system can be sold
Time-to-prototypeTime to build a working version, which may be bigger or costlier than the final product
TMS320C54xTexas Instruments DSP family; the C549 has 32 K × 16 RAM and delivers 100 MIPS at 0.45 mA/MIPS
Top-down designFrom description of the system to concrete details
Unit costThe monetary cost of manufacturing each copy, excluding NRE
Von Neumann architectureA single memory and bus for both program and data; simpler, but instruction and data accesses compete

Compiled from the ESD Module 1 deck (125 slides) and the BCSE305L Module 3 deck (49 slides), with architecture diagrams extracted directly from the source presentations. Concept explanations, theory and situation-based questions and their model answers are original work built to match the CAT-1 answer-key format; the underlying course content follows the module decks. Where this compendium disagrees with a slide, the disagreement is flagged in a grey note. Previous-year questions are from CAT-1 August 2026 (D1+TD1), questions 1, 2 and 5. Companion volume: the Module 2 compendium covering I/O interfacing techniques.
